contextual_kc_draft.text: Naïve Bayes classifiers handle missing values in the training set by ignoring the missing values of every attribute while computing its conditional probability estimates. For test instances, the classifier effectively handles missing values by using only the non-missing attribute values while computing posterior probabilities. This approach works because the classifier can easily work with incomplete information about data instances, when only a subset of attributes are observed at every instance. If only p out of d attributes are observed at a data instance, the classifier can still compute P(y) Π_{i=1}^{p} P(x_i|y) using those p attributes and choose the class with the maximum value. In the extreme case where no attributes are observed, the classifier can still use the prior probability P(y) as an estimate of the posterior probability. As more attributes are observed, the posterior probability can be refined to better reflect the likelihood of observing the data instance. This approach will not accurately estimate posterior probabilities if the frequency of missing values for a particular attribute value depends on class label.

Comparing the NB approach to general data preprocessing strategies like imputation or discarding.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming Naive Bayes requires imputation of missing values before training.
Confusing the NB approach with decision tree methods like surrogate splits or probabilistic splits.
Believing that missing values are treated as a separate categorical value in NB.

what_tutor_should_explain: The mechanism of ignoring missing values during training and using only non-missing values during testing.
The mathematical justification for using a subset of attributes in the posterior probability calculation.
The limitation that this approach fails if missingness is correlated with the class label.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A decision tree classifier can handle missing attribute values in a number of ways, both in the training and the test sets. When there are missing values in the test set, the classifier must decide which branch to follow if the value of a splitting node attribute is missing for a given test instance. One approach, known as the probabilistic split method, which is employed by the C4.5 decision tree classifier, distributes the data instance to every child of the splitting node according to the probability that the missing attribute has a particular value. In contrast, the CART algorithm uses the surrogate split method, where the instance whose splitting attribute value is missing is assigned to one of the child nodes based on the value of another non-missing surrogate attribute whose splits most resemble the partitions made by the missing attribute. Another approach, known as the separate class method is used by the CHAID algorithm, where the missing value is treated as a separate categorical value distinct from other values of the splitting attribute. Figure 3.18 shows an example of the three different ways for handling missing values in a decision tree classifier. Other strategies for dealing with missing values are based on data preprocessing, where the instance with missing value is either imputed with the mode (for categorical attribute) or mean (for continuous attribute) value or discarded before the classifier is trained.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: One of the useful properties of the naïve Bayes classifier is that it can easily work with incomplete information about data instances, when only a subset of attributes are observed at every instance. For example, if we only observe p out of $d$ attributes at a data instance, then we can still compute $\mathsf { P } ( \mathsf { y } ) \Pi \mathsf { i } { = } 1 \mathsf { p } \mathsf { P } ( \mathsf { x i } | \mathsf { y } )$ using those p attributes and choose the class with the maximum value. The naïve Bayes classifier can thus naturally handle missing values in test instances. In fact, in the extreme case where no attributes are observed, we can still use the prior probability $P ( y )$ as an estimate of the posterior probability. As we observe more attributes, we can keep refining the posterior probability to better reflect the likelihood of observing the data instance.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
A confusion matrix is a table that summarizes the performance of a classifier by comparing predicted labels against the true labels of instances in a test set. It is the most basic approach for representing classification performance and provides a concise, detailed representation of how a model predicts correctly or incorrectly. For a binary classification problem, the matrix is organized with rows representing the true class and columns representing the predicted class. The four entries in the matrix are defined as follows: True Positives (TP) are instances where the actual class is positive and the predicted class is positive; False Negatives (FN) are instances where the actual class is positive but the predicted class is negative; False Positives (FP) are instances where the actual class is negative but the predicted class is positive; and True Negatives (TN) are instances where the actual class is negative and the predicted class is negative. 

The confusion matrix is used to evaluate models on test sets that are independent of the training sets, ensuring the model can accurately predict class labels for instances it has never encountered before. While the matrix provides the information needed to determine how well a classification model performs, it is often difficult to interpret and compare the performance of classifiers using the four-dimensional representations provided by the counts. Consequently, the counts in the confusion matrix are often summarized using evaluation measures, such as accuracy, which combines these four counts into a single value. Accuracy is used extensively when classes are balanced, but it is not suitable for data sets with imbalanced class distributions because it tends to favor classifiers that correctly classify the majority class. In such cases, other measures that capture different criteria of performance are used. The confusion matrix is also applicable in contexts where classes are not equally important, and it can be used to provide the most detailed information in cluster analysis, similar to its role in classification.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, formula, and limitations of accuracy.
Specific worked examples (e.g., Accuracy = 0.700) are omitted as they are instance-specific rather than general definitions.
Confidence interval formulas are excluded as they belong to the rival unit 'Confidence Interval for Accuracy'.
contextual_kc_draft.text: Accuracy is a fundamental evaluation metric used to assess the quality of classification models and rules. In the context of binary classification, it is formally defined as the ratio of correct predictions to the total number of predictions. This is expressed by the formula: Accuracy = (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN), where TP represents true positives, TN represents true negatives, FP represents false positives, and FN represents false negatives. An equivalent general definition states that accuracy is the number of correct predictions divided by the number of all predictions. In the evaluation of specific classification rules, accuracy (also referred to as the confidence factor) is defined as the fraction of instances triggered by the rule whose class labels match the predicted class. Accuracy serves as a baseline for comparing different classification methods; however, a raw accuracy difference between two classifiers is not automatically a significant win. Statistical tests, such as a Z-statistic, are used to determine if one classifier is significantly better than another. Furthermore, measured accuracy is an estimate based on a finite test set and is subject to sampling uncertainty. Accuracy can be misleading, particularly under class imbalance, as it may hide poor performance on the positive class. In such cases, other metrics like precision and recall are often necessary to provide a more complete evaluation.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Deriving the accuracy formula from the confusion matrix components.
Comparing accuracy with precision to highlight the impact of class imbalance.
Explaining why statistical significance tests are needed when comparing classifier accuracies.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming a higher raw accuracy always means a significantly better classifier.
Using accuracy as the sole metric for imbalanced datasets, which can hide poor positive-class performance.
Confusing accuracy with precision or recall.
red_flags: Claiming that accuracy is always the best metric for classification.
Ignoring the distinction between measured accuracy and true accuracy due to sampling noise.
Failing to mention the limitations of accuracy in imbalanced scenarios.
what_tutor_should_explain: The formula for accuracy in binary classification: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN).
That accuracy is the fraction of correct predictions out of all predictions.
That accuracy can be misleading under class imbalance.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Precision is an evaluation measure for binary classification that quantifies the fraction of correct predictions of the positive class over the total number of positive predictions. It is also referred to as the positive predicted value (PPV). The standard formula for precision is p = TP / (TP + FP), where TP represents true positives and FP represents false positives. A classifier with high precision is likely to have most of its positive predictions correct, making it a useful measure for highly skewed test sets where positive predictions, even though small in numbers, are required to be mostly correct. Precision is sensitive to class skew; when selecting a score threshold for a classifier optimized for precision, the skew of the validation set should be similar to that of the test set to ensure optimal performance. In the context of statistical testing, precision is closely related to the false discovery rate (FDR), with the relationship precision = 1 - FDR. Precision captures the effect of false positives but not false negatives; a classifier that is very conservative in classifying instances as positive to reduce false positives may achieve high precision but very poor recall. A perfect classifier is characterized by precision = 1 and recall = 1.

Ignoring the impact of class skew on precision when evaluating classifiers.
red_flags: Stating that precision is insensitive to class skew.
Defining precision as TP / (TP + FN).
Claiming that a classifier with high precision must also have high recall.
Failing to distinguish between precision and FDR.

Hence, if we optimize only one of these evaluation measures, we may end up with a classifier that shows low FN but high FP, or vice-versa. For example, a classifier that declares every instance to be positive will have a perfect recall, but high FPR and very poor precision. On the other hand, a classifier that is very conservative in classifying an instance as positive (to reduce FP) may end up having high precision but very poor recall. We thus need evaluation measures that account for both types of misclassifications, FP and FN. Some examples of such evaluation measures are summarized by the following definitions.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Recall, also known as sensitivity, is a classifier evaluation metric that measures the proportion of actual positive instances correctly identified by the model. In the medical community, this metric is referred to as sensitivity, while in the information retrieval literature, it is called recall. A classifier with a high recall value has a high chance of correctly identifying the positive instances in the data. The metric is calculated using the formula: Recall = TP / (TP + FN), where TP represents true positives and FN represents false negatives. In a specific evaluation example, a classifier with 2 true positives and 1 false negative yields a recall of 2/3, or approximately 0.667 (66.7%). This value is identical to the sensitivity calculated for the same dataset, confirming that sensitivity and recall are equivalent metrics. The calculation relies on the confusion matrix components, specifically the count of true positives and false negatives, to determine the model's ability to capture all relevant positive cases.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Specificity, also known as the true negative rate (TNR), is a classifier evaluation metric defined as the fraction of negative test instances correctly predicted by the classifier. Formally, it is calculated as the number of true negatives (TN) divided by the sum of true negatives and false positives (FP), expressed as Specificity = TN / (TN + FP). In this formula, TN represents the count of actual negative cases correctly identified as negative, and FP represents the count of actual negative cases incorrectly identified as positive. Specificity checks how many actual negatives were correctly rejected, distinguishing it from precision, which checks the quality of positive predictions, and accuracy, which counts all correct predictions. It is not the same as precision for the negative class because specificity uses actual negatives in the denominator, whereas negative predictive value would use predicted negatives. In a worked example, a classifier with 5 true negatives and 2 false positives yields a specificity of 5/7, or approximately 71.4%.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The confusion matrix provides a concise representation of classification performance on a given test data set. However, it is often difficult to interpret and compare the performance of classifiers using the four-dimensional representations (corresponding to the four counts) provided by their confusion matrices. Hence, the counts in the confusion matrix are often summarized using a number of evaluation measures . Accuracy is an example of one such measure that combines these four counts into a single value, which is used extensively when classes are balanced. However, the accuracy measure is not suitable for handling data sets with imbalanced class distributions as it tends to favor classifiers that correctly classify the majority class. In the following, we describe other possible measures that capture different criteria of performance when working with imbalanced classes.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Random subsampling is a model evaluation technique that repeats random hold-out splits several times and averages the results. It is more stable than a single hold-out split but does not guarantee that every instance is tested exactly once; some instances may be tested repeatedly while others may not be tested. This method is distinct from cross-validation, which splits data into k folds and trains on k−1 folds while testing on the remaining fold, repeating until each fold has been tested once. It is also distinct from bootstrap sampling, which samples N instances with replacement to form training sets and evaluates on out-of-bag instances. Random subsampling is a specific variation of random sampling where the probability of selecting any particular object is equal, and it can be performed with or without replacement. Sampling with replacement is simpler to analyze because the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: There are many sampling techniques, but only a few of the most basic ones and their variations will be covered here. The simplest type of sampling is simple random sampling . For this type of sampling, there is an equal probability of selecting any particular object. There are two variations on random sampling (and other sampling techniques as well): (1) sampling without replacement -as each object is selected, it is removed from the set of all objects that together constitute the population , and (2) sampling with replacement -objects are not removed from the population as they are selected for the sample. In sampling with replacement, the same object can be picked more than once. The samples produced by the two methods are not much different when samples are relatively small compared to the data set size, but sampling with replacement is simpler to analyze because the probability of selecting any object remains constant during the sampling process.

The draft distinguishes k-fold cross-validation from holdout, leave-one-out, and stratified cross-validation.
contextual_kc_draft.text: k-Fold Cross Validation is a model evaluation technique that generalizes the holdout approach by segmenting the labeled data D (of size N) into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. During the i-th run, one partition is chosen as the test set (D.test(i)) while the remaining k-1 partitions are used as the training set (D.train(i)). This process is repeated until each fold has been used for testing exactly once. A different model is learned at every run, and the performance of each model on its respective test fold is aggregated to compute the overall test error rate. This aggregated rate reflects the expected generalization error of the model selection approach when applied to a training set of the same size as one of the training folds, rather than the performance of a single specific model. The choice of k depends on problem characteristics: a small k results in smaller training sets and a larger estimate of generalization error, while a high k reduces bias by using larger training sets. For most practical applications, k between 5 and 10 is reasonable, allowing each fold to use 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training. An extreme case is the leave-one-out approach (k=N), which maximizes training data but is computationally expensive and cannot estimate the variance of the error rate. Standard k-fold cross-validation does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition matches the overall data distribution; this limitation is addressed by stratified cross-validation, which performs stratified sampling to preserve class distribution. The method is also used for hyper-parameter selection, where the fold is used for validation and the remainder for training, selecting the hyper-parameter value that provides the lowest validation error rate before learning the final model on the entire training set.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The right choice of k in k-fold cross-validation depends on a number of characteristics of the problem. A small value of k will result in a smaller training set at every run, which will result in a larger estimate of generalization error rate than what is expected of a model trained over the entire labeled set. On the other hand, a high value of k results in a larger training set at every run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate. In the extreme case, when , every run uses exactly one data instance for testingk=N and the remainder of the data for testing. This special case of k-fold crossvalidation is called the leave-one-out approach. This approach has the advantage of utilizing as much data as possible for training. Furthermore, leave-one-out can be computationally expensive for large data sets as the cross-validation procedure needs to be repeated N times. For most practical applications, the choice of k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating the generalization error rate, because each fold is able to make use of 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training.

For example, a common approach for generating new data sets is to use bootstrap sampling, where data instances are randomly selected with replacement such that the resultant data set is of the same size as the original set. For classification, an alternative to bootstrap sampling is k -fold crossvalidation, where the data set is systematically split into subsets for k number of times. As we will see later in Section 10.3.1 , such statistical resampling approaches are used to compute distributions of measures of classification performance, such as accuracy, precision, and recall. evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Another type of analysis relevant to predictive models, such as classification, is to model the distribution of various measures of classification performance. One way to estimate such distributions is to generate bootstrap samples from the labeled data (preserving the original labels) to create new training and test sets. The performance of a classification model trained and evaluated on a number of these bootstrapped data sets can then be used to generate a distribution for the measure of interest. Another way to create the alternative distribution would be to use the randomized cross-validation procedure (discussed in Section 3.6.2 ) where the process of randomly partitioning the labeled data into k folds is repeated multiple times.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, the formal condition (k=N), the procedure, and the primary limitations (computational cost and variance estimation) supported by the evidence.
contextual_kc_draft.text: Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) is a special case of k-fold cross-validation where the number of folds k equals the total number of data instances N. In this approach, the cross-validation procedure is repeated N times; in each run, the model is trained on N − 1 instances and tested on the single remaining instance. This configuration ensures that every data instance is used exactly once as a test case and that each training set is as large as possible, which reduces the bias in the estimate of the generalization error rate compared to smaller values of k. However, LOOCV is computationally expensive for large data sets because the model must be trained N times. Additionally, because there is only one possible partitioning of the data for the leave-one-out approach, it is not possible to estimate the variance of the generalization error rate, which is a limitation of this method compared to approaches that use multiple random partitionings.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The right choice of k in k-fold cross-validation depends on a number of characteristics of the problem. A small value of k will result in a smaller training set at every run, which will result in a larger estimate of generalization error rate than what is expected of a model trained over the entire labeled set. On the other hand, a high value of k results in a larger training set at every run, which reduces the bias in the estimate of generalization error rate. In the extreme case, when , every run uses exactly one data instance for testingk=N and the remainder of the data for testing. This special case of k-fold crossvalidation is called the leave-one-out approach. Furthermore, leave-one-out can be computationally expensive for large data sets as the cross-validation procedure needs to be repeated N times. For most practical applications, the choice of k between 5 and 10 provides a reasonable approach for estimating the generalization error rate, because each fold is able to make use of 80% to 90% of the labeled data for training.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Bootstrap sampling is a statistical resampling technique used to generate synthetic collections of data instances by randomly sampling from an original data set with replacement. In this process, data instances are selected such that the resultant data set is of the same size as the original set. Because the sampling is done with replacement, some instances may appear several times in the same training set, while others may be omitted. On average, a bootstrap sample of size N contains approximately 63.2% of the unique instances in the original data, leaving about 36.8% of the instances unselected. These unselected instances are referred to as out-of-bag instances and can be used as a test set for model evaluation. The bootstrap procedure is often repeated multiple times to compute distributions of measures of classification performance, such as accuracy, precision, and recall, or to estimate the distribution of the support of a frequent itemset. These distributions can then be used to produce confidence intervals for these measures. In the context of ensemble methods like random forests, bootstrap sampling is used to create diversity among trees by providing different training data for each tree, which helps reduce correlation between them.

For example, a common approach for generating new data sets is to use bootstrap sampling, where data instances are randomly selected with replacement such that the resultant data set is of the same size as the original set. We can also use these distributions to produce confidence intervals for these measures.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Another type of analysis relevant to predictive models, such as classification, is to model the distribution of various measures of classification performance. One way to estimate such distributions is to generate bootstrap samples from the labeled data (preserving the original labels) to create new training and test sets. The performance of a classification model trained and evaluated on a number of these bootstrapped data sets can then be used to generate a distribution for the measure of interest. Another way to create the alternative distribution would be to use the randomized cross-validation procedure (discussed in Section 3.6.2 ) where the process of randomly partitioning the labeled data into k folds is repeated multiple times.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, the procedure (stratified sampling into folds), the motivation (preserving class distribution), and the empirical recommendation for 10-fold stratified CV.
The draft distinguishes this unit from standard k-fold cross validation by highlighting the stratification step.
contextual_kc_draft.text: Stratified k-fold cross validation is a model evaluation technique that extends standard k-fold cross validation by ensuring that each fold approximately preserves the class distribution of the full dataset. In standard k-fold cross validation, the labeled data is segmented into k equal-sized partitions, or folds. During each run, one partition is used for testing while the remaining k-1 partitions are used for training. This process is repeated until every fold has served as the test set exactly once. A key limitation of standard k-fold cross validation is that it does not guarantee that the fraction of positive and negative instances in every partition is equal to the fraction observed in the overall data. Stratified cross validation addresses this by performing a stratified sampling of the positive and negative instances into the k partitions. This ensures that the proportion of class labels in every fold is kept the same as that of the overall data. For example, if the full dataset contains a specific ratio of classes, each fold will maintain that ratio. This approach is often preferred because it preserves class proportions in each fold, which is particularly important for imbalanced datasets. An empirical study by Kohavi suggests that ten-fold stratified cross validation is the best estimation method for performance metrics compared to random subsampling and other methods. The method is computationally more expensive than simple hold-out methods but provides a more robust estimate of generalization error by utilizing every data instance for both training and testing across the k runs.

common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing stratified k-fold with standard k-fold, where class distribution is not guaranteed in each fold.
Assuming that the test error rate from stratified k-fold reflects the performance of a single specific model rather than the expected generalization error of the model selection approach.
Believing that stratification is only necessary for binary classification, whereas it applies to multi-class distributions as well.

Claiming that the aggregated error rate represents the performance of a single model trained on the full dataset.
Omitting the step of repeating the process until each fold has been used for testing once.

contextual_kc_draft.text: An ensemble classifier is a model that combines several base classifiers to make a single final prediction. The base classifiers are often individually imperfect, but their combined decision can be more robust. For classification, a common combination rule is majority voting, where the predicted class is the majority of the individual predictions: ŷ = majority{h1(x), h2(x),..., hB(x)}. An alternate approach is a weighted majority vote, where the weight of a base classifier denotes its accuracy or relevance. The ensemble of classifiers can be constructed in many ways, including by manipulating the training set. In this approach, multiple training sets are created by resampling the original data according to some sampling distribution and constructing a classifier from each training set. Bagging and boosting are two examples of ensemble methods that manipulate their training sets. The base classifiers for most of these approaches can be generated sequentially (one after another) or in parallel (all at once). Once an ensemble of classifiers has been learned, a test example is classified by combining the predictions made by the base classifiers. The ensemble classifier predicts the class label of a test example by taking a majority vote on the predictions made by the base classifiers. If the base classifiers are identical, then all the base classifiers will commit the same mistakes, and the error rate of the ensemble remains the same as the base classifiers. On the other hand, if the base classifiers are independent—i.e., their errors are uncorrelated—then the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly. The ensemble classifier performs worse than the base classifiers when the base classifier error rate is larger than 0.5. Two necessary conditions for an ensemble classifier to perform better than a single classifier are: (1) the base classifiers should be independent of each other, and (2) the base classifiers should do better than a classifier that performs random guessing. contextual_kc_draft.text: Majority voting is a combination rule used in ensemble classification to derive a single final prediction from the outputs of multiple base classifiers. In this approach, each base classifier predicts a class label for a given instance, and the final prediction is the class that receives the most votes. This method is commonly applied in random forests, where a test instance is passed through all trees in the ensemble, and the class with the highest number of votes becomes the forest's prediction. The rule is particularly effective when the base classifiers are diverse and their errors are not perfectly correlated; if the classifiers are identical, they will make the same mistakes, and the ensemble's error rate will not improve over that of a single classifier. Conversely, when classifiers are independent, the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly, which can significantly reduce the overall error rate. In binary classification, majority voting is equivalent to summing the predicted values and examining the sign of the resulting sum. An alternative to simple majority voting is weighted majority voting, where each base classifier's vote is weighted according to its accuracy or relevance, allowing more reliable classifiers to have a greater influence on the final decision. In the context of k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns a test instance to the class that appears most frequently among its nearest neighbors, with each neighbor having equal impact on the classification. This contrasts with distance-weighted voting, where the influence of each neighbor is weighted by its distance to the test instance. Majority voting is a foundational technique in ensemble methods, providing a simple and effective way to combine the predictions of multiple models to improve classification accuracy and robustness.

If base classifiers are identical, the ensemble's error rate will not improve over that of a single classifier.
When base classifiers are independent, the ensemble makes a wrong prediction only if more than half of the base classifiers predict incorrectly.
In binary classification, majority voting is equivalent to summing the predicted values and examining the sign of the resulting sum.
An alternative to simple majority voting is weighted majority voting, where each base classifier's vote is weighted according to its accuracy or relevance.
In k-nearest neighbors, majority voting assigns a test instance to the class that appears most frequently among its nearest neighbors, with each neighbor having equal impact.
Distance-weighted voting weights the influence of each neighbor by its distance to the test instance, contrasting with majority voting.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, induction procedure, prediction rule, hyper-parameters, and properties of random forests as supported by the evidence.

The out-of-bag error estimate is mentioned as a method for hyper-parameter selection, but the specific steps for computing it are not detailed in the provided evidence passages, so it is described conceptually rather than procedurally.
contextual_kc_draft.text: A random forest is an ensemble method that uses decision trees as its base classifiers. It is distinguished from simple bagging by manipulating both the training instances and the input features: each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample of the training data, and at every internal node, the best splitting criterion is chosen from a randomly selected subset of attributes. This dual randomness creates diversity among the trees and reduces correlation between their predictions. The induction process involves building B trees, where for each tree, a bootstrap sample of N instances is drawn with replacement, and a decision tree is grown using random feature selection at each split. The trees are typically grown deeply without heavy pruning, resulting in base classifiers that have low bias but high variance. For classification, the final prediction is made by majority voting over the predictions of all B trees. This aggregation reduces the variance of the individual trees without negatively impacting their low bias, making random forests robust to overfitting and computationally efficient even in high-dimensional settings. The number of attributes selected at each node, denoted as p, is a hyper-parameter that balances the strength of individual trees against their correlation; a small p reduces correlation but may weaken individual trees, while a large p improves strength but may result in correlated trees similar to bagging. An alternative to tuning p on a validation set is the out-of-bag (oob) error estimate, which computes a reliable estimate of the generalization error rate directly during training by using instances not included in the bootstrap sample for a given tree.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Explaining the analogy of an ensemble as asking several models to vote, where the majority vote is more reliable if the models make different mistakes.
Using the concept of 'decorrelated' decision trees to explain why random forests reduce variance.
Describing the out-of-bag error estimate as a way to use 'unused' data from the bootstrap process for validation.
Contrasting random forest with bagging to highlight the additional benefit of random feature selection.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing random forest with simple bagging, ignoring the random feature selection component.
Believing that each individual tree in a random forest is better than a normal tree, rather than understanding that the ensemble of diverse, noisy trees works better.
Thinking that random forests prune their trees heavily, when in fact they often grow trees deeply and rely on ensemble averaging to control overfitting.
Misunderstanding the role of the hyper-parameter p, thinking a larger p is always better without considering the increased correlation among trees.
red_flags: Stating that random forests work because each tree is better than a normal tree.
Omitting the random feature selection component when describing random forest induction.
Claiming that random forests are always superior to boosting without acknowledging that their performance is often comparable and that random forests are more robust to overfitting and faster.
Failing to mention that the base classifiers in random forests are unpruned and have high variance.
what_tutor_should_explain: The two main random components: bootstrap sampling of instances and random feature selection at each split.
How the combination of these random components creates diversity and reduces correlation among the trees.
The induction process: drawing bootstrap samples, growing trees with random feature subsets, and combining predictions via majority voting.
The role of the hyper-parameter p (number of attributes selected at each node) and its trade-off between tree strength and correlation.
The concept of out-of-bag error estimation as a way to evaluate generalization performance without a separate validation set.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A random forest is induced by building many decision trees. The main random components are therefore the bootstrap sampling of training instances and the random selection of candidate attributes at each split.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
Boosting is an iterative ensemble procedure that adaptively changes the distribution of training examples so that base classifiers increasingly focus on examples that are hard to classify. Unlike bagging, boosting assigns a weight to each training example and may adaptively change the weight at the end of each boosting round. The weights determine the sampling distribution used to create training sets; examples that are classified incorrectly have their weights increased, while those classified correctly have their weights decreased. As boosting rounds proceed, examples that are the hardest to classify tend to become more prevalent in the training sets. The final ensemble is obtained by aggregating the base classifiers obtained from each boosting round.

The general procedure is: (1) initially assign equal weights (1/N) to all examples; (2) draw a sample according to the sampling distribution to obtain a new training set; (3) build a classifier from the training set and use it to classify all examples in the original data; (4) update the weights of the training examples at the end of the round, increasing weights for incorrectly classified examples and decreasing weights for correctly classified ones; and (5) repeat the process for subsequent rounds.

Several implementations of boosting differ in how weights are updated and how predictions are combined. In AdaBoost, the weight update mechanism increases the weights of incorrectly classified examples and decreases the weights of those classified correctly, using a normalization factor to ensure the weights sum to 1. Instead of using a majority voting scheme, the prediction made by each classifier is weighted, allowing AdaBoost to penalize models that have poor accuracy. If any intermediate rounds produce an error rate higher than 50%, the weights are reverted back to their original uniform values, and the resampling procedure is repeated. The training error of the ensemble decreases exponentially, leading to fast convergence. However, because of its tendency to focus on training examples that are wrongly classified, the boosting technique can be susceptible to overfitting, resulting in poor generalization performance in some scenarios.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The class imbalance problem occurs when a training set has an unbalanced representation of classes, typically with a minority class that is not well-represented. This condition poses two challenges for classification: many standard classification methods work well only when the training set has a balanced representation of both classes, and classifiers trained on imbalanced data generally show a bias toward improving performance over the majority class, which is often not the desired behavior. Although some classifiers, such as rule-based classifiers and k-NN, are more effective at handling imbalance than others, they are all impacted if the minority class is poorly represented. In the context of binary classification, the minority class is referred to as the positive class and the majority class as the negative class. The problem also affects model evaluation because standard metrics like detection rate and false alarm rate are not sensitive to skewness in the class distribution. Consequently, in the presence of class imbalance, the behavior of an algorithm over small false positive rate values (early retrieval) is often more meaningful for comparison than performance over all operating points. The precision-recall (PR) curve is an alternate approach for measuring aggregate performance that is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance, as it generally provides deeper insight into classifier performance than ROC curves, particularly in the early retrieval range.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A method for comparing classifier performance using the convex hull of ROC curves was suggested by Provost and Fawcett in [ 286 ]. Bradley [ 208 ] investigated the use of area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms. For example, the AUC can be used to compare the quality of two classifiers only if the ROC curve of one classifier strictly dominates the other. However, if the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect at any point, then it is difficult to assess the relative quality of classifiers using the AUC measure. An in-depth discussion of the pitfalls in using AUC as a performance measure can be obtained in works by Hand [ 245 , 246 ], and Powers [ 284 ]. The AUC has also been considered to be an incoherent measure of performance, i.e., it uses different scales while comparing the performance of different classifiers, although a coherent interpretation of AUC has been provided by Ferri et al. Berrar and Flach [ 203 ] describe some of the common caveats in using the ROC curve for clinical microarray research. An alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier is the precision-recall (PR) curve, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance [ 292 ].

contextual_kc_draft.text:
Oversampling is a technique used to address class imbalance by creating a balanced training set through the artificial generation of new positive examples. A simple approach involves duplicating every positive instance a specific number of times, calculated as the ratio of negative to positive instances (n−/n+). This duplication is analogous to doubling the weight of positive instances during training, an effect that can alternatively be achieved by assigning higher weights to positive instances than negative instances in classifiers such as logistic regression, artificial neural networks, and support vector machines. In the context of decision trees, oversampling provides the additional examples needed to ensure that decision boundaries surrounding positive examples are not pruned, thereby improving the classification of minority class instances that might otherwise be misclassified due to insufficient representation.

The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) is an alternative approach designed to overcome the limitations of simple duplication. A key limitation of the duplication method is that replicated positive examples have an artificially lower variance compared to their true distribution, which can bias the classifier to the specific distribution of training instances and lead to poor generalizability. To address this, SMOTE generates synthetic positive instances in the neighborhood of existing positive instances. The procedure for SMOTE involves first determining the k-nearest positive neighbors of every positive instance. Then, a synthetic positive instance is generated at some intermediate point along the line segment joining a positive instance to one of its randomly chosen k-nearest neighbors. This process is repeated until the desired number of positive instances is reached. However, SMOTE has a specific limitation: it can only generate new positive instances within the convex hull of the existing positive class. Consequently, it does not help improve the representation of the positive class outside the boundary of existing positive instances. Despite their complementary strengths and weaknesses, undersampling and oversampling provide useful directions for generating balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Undersampling is a sampling method used to create balanced training sets in the presence of class imbalance by reducing the frequency of the majority class to match the frequency of the minority class. This approach is one of two primary sampling strategies for ensuring adequate representation of both majority and minority classes during classifier training, the other being oversampling. To illustrate the procedure, consider a training set containing 100 positive examples and 1000 negative examples. To overcome the skew among the classes, a random sample of 100 examples is selected from the negative class and used with the 100 positive examples to create a balanced training set. Despite its utility, undersampling has specific limitations. One limitation is that some useful negative examples, particularly those closer to the actual decision boundary, may not be chosen for training, which can result in an inferior classification model. Another limitation is that the smaller sample of negative instances may have a higher variance than the larger original set. Undersampling and oversampling provide complementary directions for generating balanced training sets, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The cost matrix is a framework for evaluating cost-sensitive decision quality by assigning specific values to the consequences of different types of decisions. In this evaluation context, the matrix allows for the calculation of expected cost per instance, which depends on the prior probability of the class, the false positive rate, the true positive rate, and the specific cost values assigned to outcomes. For example, a cost value for true positives can be negative, meaning that correctly identifying a positive case reduces the total cost. The cost matrix is used to determine the best model based on the real consequences of each type of decision, which may differ from models selected by other metrics like ROC/AUC or F1. In one exercise, a model with the lowest expected cost was selected as the best, even though it was not the best by other metrics. The cost matrix is distinct from the confusion matrix, which counts the number of each type of decision, and from the similarity matrix, which measures the similarity between data points. The cost matrix is also distinct from the class imbalance problem, which is the problem of having unequal numbers of cases in different classes, and from cost-sensitive classification, which is the general approach of incorporating cost information into the learning algorithm.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Cost-Sensitive Classification is an approach to model evaluation and learning that accounts for the differing consequences of misclassification errors. It is motivated by the need for alternative evaluation metrics that are sensitive to class skew and capture performance criteria beyond standard accuracy. In this framework, decision quality is evaluated using a cost matrix, which assigns specific costs to different types of errors. The method involves incorporating cost information into the learning process or evaluation, with techniques ranging from algorithm-specific modifications to algorithm-independent methods. A worked example demonstrates that cost-sensitive evaluation can select a model based on the lowest expected cost, distinguishing it from metrics that evaluate ranking quality across thresholds.

contextual_kc_draft.text: RIPPER is a widely used rule induction algorithm that implements a direct method for generating classification rules directly from data, distinguishing it from indirect methods that derive rules from decision trees. It is designed to work well with noisy data by using a validation set to prevent model overfitting. The algorithm typically employs a sequential covering scheme to induce rules. After generating a rule, RIPPER eliminates all positive and negative examples covered by that rule. The rule is added to the rule set only if it does not violate specific stopping conditions. One stopping condition is based on the minimum description length principle: if a new rule increases the total description length of the rule set by at least d bits (where d defaults to 64 bits), RIPPER stops adding rules. Another stopping condition requires that the error rate of the rule on the validation set must not exceed 50%. RIPPER also prunes rules to improve generalization errors based on their performance on the validation set. Pruning is done starting from the last conjunct added to the rule; if a metric related to the rule's accuracy improves after removing a conjunct, that conjunct is removed. While the original rule covers only positive examples, the pruned rule may cover some negative examples in the training set.
uncertainty_notes: The exact formula for the pruning metric is missing from the evidence (rendered as a placeholder), preventing a complete formal description of the pruning step.

Holte's 1R [ 255 ] is the simplest form of a rule-based classifier because its rule set contains only a single rule. Other examples of rulebased classifiers include IREP [ 234 ], RIPPER [ 218 ], CN2 [ 216 , 217 ], AQ [ 276 ], RISE [ 224 ], and ITRULE [ 296 ]. Table 4.8 shows a comparison of the characteristics of four of these classifiers.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
A confidence interval for accuracy is an interval of parameter values in which an estimated accuracy value is guaranteed to fall a certain percentage of times, known as the confidence level. It is used to quantify the inherent uncertainty in a classifier's performance because accuracy measured on a finite test set is only an estimate. The interval is often reported along with point estimates to express how much the true accuracy could plausibly differ due to sampling variation.

The derivation of the confidence interval for accuracy models the classification task as a binomial random experiment. Given a test set of N instances, let X be the number of instances correctly predicted and p be the true accuracy. The empirical accuracy is defined as acc = X/N. The binomial distribution for X has a mean of Np and a variance of Np(1-p). The empirical accuracy acc has a binomial distribution with mean p and variance p(1-p)/N. When N is sufficiently large, the binomial distribution can be approximated by a normal distribution, which allows the confidence interval for acc to be derived.

The general form of the confidence interval is the estimate plus or minus an uncertainty margin. For a 90% two-sided interval, the formula uses the Z-value Z0.95 = 1.64. Larger test sets produce smaller standard errors, resulting in a narrower confidence interval. In a specific example, a model with an accuracy of 80% evaluated on 100 test instances yields a confidence interval between 71.1% and 86.7% at a 95% confidence level, where the Z-value is 1.96.
uncertainty_notes: The exact formula for the confidence interval (e.g., acc ± Z * sqrt(p(1-p)/N)) is not explicitly written out in the evidence, only described as 'estimate ± uncertainty margin' and referencing a Z-value.

The evidence contains a potential inconsistency or specific context regarding the Z-value: one passage states 'For a 90% two-sided interval, the formula uses Z0.95 = 1.64', while another example uses Z=1.96 for 95% confidence. The draft reflects the specific values provided in the text without resolving the statistical convention, as the text explicitly links 90% confidence to Z0.95=1.64 in one context and 95% to Z=1.96 in another.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Explaining that accuracy measured on a finite test set is an estimate and the confidence interval quantifies the uncertainty.
Demonstrating how larger test sets produce smaller standard errors and narrower confidence intervals.
Using the binomial experiment model to derive the confidence interval for accuracy.

Clarifying the role of the Z-value in determining the width of the confidence interval.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the confidence interval for accuracy with the accuracy point estimate itself.

Misinterpreting the confidence level as the probability that the true accuracy is within the interval for a specific sample, rather than the long-run frequency of the interval containing the true value.
Using the wrong Z-value for a given confidence level (e.g., using Z=1.28 for 90% confidence instead of Z=1.64 as specified in the evidence for a two-sided interval).
Assuming that a higher raw accuracy alone is a significant win without considering the confidence interval and sampling uncertainty.
Failing to account for the sampling variation when interpreting a single accuracy measurement.
red_flags: Stating that the confidence interval is the exact true accuracy of the classifier.
Ignoring the sampling uncertainty when comparing models based on accuracy alone.
Using an incorrect Z-value for the specified confidence level.
Failing to mention that the confidence interval is derived under the assumption of a normal approximation to the binomial distribution.
Confusing the confidence interval for a single model's accuracy with the confidence interval for the difference between two models' accuracies.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Such resampling approaches can also help in estimating confidence intervals for measures of the true performance of the classifier trained over all possible instances. A confidence interval is an interval of parameter values in which an estimated parameter value is guaranteed to fall a certain percentage of times. The confidence level is the percentage of times the estimated parameter will fall within the interval. For example, given the distribution of a classifier's accuracy, we can estimate the interval of values that contains 95% of the distribution. This serves as the confidence interval of the classifier's true accuracy at the 95% confidence level. To quantify the inherent uncertainty in the result, confidence intervals are often reported along with point estimates of a model's output.

The confidence level is the percentage of times the estimated parameter will fall within the interval. For example, given the distribution of a classifier's accuracy, we can estimate the interval of values that contains 95% of the distribution. This serves as the confidence interval of the classifier's true accuracy at the 95% confidence level. To quantify the inherent uncertainty in the result, confidence intervals are often reported along with point estimates of a model's output.

coverage_notes: The evidence defines the problem and variables but does not provide the specific statistical test (e.g., t-test, z-test) or formula for calculating significance.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Comparing two models on independent test sets is a statistical evaluation task used to determine whether the observed difference in performance between two classification models is statistically significant. This approach is necessary because a raw difference in accuracy or error rates may be due to random variation rather than a true difference in model quality. The setup involves two models, typically denoted as M1 and M2, which are evaluated on two distinct, independent test sets, D1 and D2. The number of instances in each test set is denoted as n1 and n2, respectively. The error rate for model M1 on test set D1 is denoted as e1, and the error rate for model M2 on test set D2 is denoted as e2. The primary goal is to test the statistical significance of the difference between e1 and e2. A key difficulty in this comparison is that the significance of the performance difference depends on the size of the test sets; for example, a model achieving 85% accuracy on a test set of 30 instances is not directly comparable in statistical confidence to a model achieving 75% accuracy on a test set of 5,000 instances. The evidence provided establishes the problem definition and the variables involved but does not specify the particular statistical test or formula used to perform the comparison.
uncertainty_notes: The specific statistical method or formula for testing the significance of the difference between the two error rates is not present in the supplied evidence.
The relationship between the test set sizes (n1, n2) and the statistical power of the test is implied by the example but not formally defined in the provided passages.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using the example of 85% accuracy on 30 instances vs 75% accuracy on 5000 instances to illustrate the difficulty of comparison.
Defining the goal as testing the statistical significance of the difference between e1 and e2.
Clarifying that the test sets D1 and D2 must be independent.
common_confusions_or_errors: Assuming that a higher accuracy on a small test set is statistically equivalent to a lower accuracy on a large test set.
Confusing the comparison of two models on independent sets with the comparison of two models on the same set (McNemar).
Ignoring the sample size when interpreting the difference in error rates.
red_flags: Claiming that a raw difference in accuracy is sufficient to declare one model superior without statistical testing.
Failing to account for the different sizes of the independent test sets in the comparison.
Applying a test designed for paired data (like McNemar) to independent test sets without justification.
what_tutor_should_explain: The necessity of statistical testing to distinguish true performance differences from random variation.
The role of test set size (n1, n2) in determining the significance of the observed error rate difference.
The definition of the variables M1, M2, D1, D2, e1, and e2 in the context of independent test sets.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The significance level, denoted by the Greek letter alpha (α), is a fixed constant in hypothesis testing whose value is decided before any tests are performed. It is defined as the probability of incurring a type I error, which is the probability of the critical region under the null hypothesis. In practice, a result is called statistically significant if it has a p-value lower than the pre-specified threshold α. Rejecting the null hypothesis if the test statistic falls in the critical region is equivalent to evaluating the p-value and rejecting the null hypothesis if the p-value falls below α. While every result has a different p-value, the significance level α remains a fixed constant. Common choices for the level of significance are 0.05 (5%) and 0.01 (1%). In the context of multiple testing, such as the Bonferroni procedure, the significance level for every individual test may be adjusted (e.g., to α/m) to control the family-wise error rate (FWER). For FDR controlling procedures, α represents the desired false discovery rate and is often chosen to have a value greater than 0.05, such as 0.20. The significance level is distinct from the p-value, which is a result-specific metric, and from the critical value, which is a threshold derived from α for a specific test statistic distribution.

coverage_notes: The evidence provides a clear definition of one-sided and two-sided tests, including the distribution of alpha across tails and specific Z-score thresholds for two-sided tests.
The evidence does not provide a specific formula or threshold for one-sided tests, only the general principle of alpha allocation.

contextual_kc_draft.text: One-sided and two-sided tests are statistical procedures used to evaluate whether an observed result is a significant departure from a null hypothesis. The test statistic, typically a count or real-valued quantity, measures how 'extreme' an observed result is under the null hypothesis. A one-sided test focuses on a specific direction of difference, such as testing whether model A is better than model B, and is categorized as either right-tailed or left-tailed. In contrast, a two-sided test asks whether the models are different in either direction. The distinction is reflected in the distribution of the significance level (alpha) across the tails of the null distribution: a two-sided test with alpha = 0.05 allocates 0.025 probability to each tail, whereas a one-sided test places the entire 0.05 probability in a single tail. A low p-value indicates smaller probabilities in the tails of the null distribution for both types of tests, providing sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. For a two-tailed test, the decision rule typically uses a threshold such as |Z| > 1.96 at alpha = 0.05, while a 90% two-sided interval uses Z0.95 = 1.64. Larger test sets produce smaller standard errors, which results in narrower confidence intervals.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a visual diagram of the null distribution to show how alpha is split between tails.
Providing a concrete example of a one-sided test (e.g., A is better than B) versus a two-sided test (A is different from B).
Explaining the relationship between test set size, standard error, and the width of the confidence interval.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the directionality of a one-sided test with the magnitude of the effect.
Misapplying the two-sided Z-score threshold to a one-sided test without adjusting for the alpha allocation.
Assuming that a two-sided test is always more conservative without considering the specific hypothesis being tested.
red_flags: Stating that a one-sided test has a higher power without explaining the directional constraint.
Using the term 'two-tailed' and 'two-sided' interchangeably without confirming they refer to the same concept in the context.
Failing to specify the alpha level when discussing Z-score thresholds.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The role of test sample size in model evaluation is defined by the direct dependence of measured accuracy on the specific test sample used. When selecting a sample size, there is a fundamental trade-off: larger sample sizes increase the probability that the sample will be representative of the underlying data, but they also eliminate much of the computational advantage of sampling. Conversely, smaller sample sizes carry the risk of missing true patterns or detecting erroneous ones. This impact on representativeness is demonstrated by a data set containing 8000 two-dimensional points, where a sample of 2000 points preserves most of the data structure, while a sample of 500 points misses much of it. In the context of cluster analysis, the probability of capturing all structures is highly sensitive to sample size; for a data set with 10 clusters, a sample size of 20 has only a 20% chance of including all clusters, and even a sample size of 30 has an almost 40% chance of missing objects from at least one cluster. These examples illustrate that sample size is a critical parameter that directly influences the reliability and representativeness of the evaluation results.

Discussing the 20% and 40% probabilities of missing clusters in small samples to highlight the risk of under-sampling.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve is a graphical tool used for the aggregate evaluation of classifiers by displaying the trade-off between the true positive rate (TPR) and the false positive rate (FPR) across varying score thresholds. In this visualization, the TPR is plotted on the y-axis and the FPR is plotted on the x-axis. Each point on the curve represents a specific operating point of the classifier, corresponding to a model generated by placing a particular threshold on the test scores produced by the classifier. Because the TPR monotonically increases as the FPR increases, the ROC curve exhibits a staircase pattern. A good ROC curve rises quickly before moving far to the right, indicating that the model catches positive instances before creating many false positives, and is generally considered better when it is closer to the top-left corner. The generic procedure for computing an ROC curve involves sorting the predictions according to their score values and then plotting the TPR and FPR for every possible value of the score threshold. This approach allows for the empirical estimation of classification performance for different score thresholds in the presence of ground truth labels, without the need for explicit statistical models or assumptions. The ROC curve facilitates the comparison of classifiers over a range of operating points, allowing users to select an operating point based on application requirements. However, if the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the area under the curve (AUC) measure, as neither classifier strictly dominates the other across all operating points. In the presence of class imbalance, the precision-recall (PR) curve is often preferred over the ROC curve because it provides deeper insight into classifier performance, particularly in the early retrieval range of operating points.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The performance of a classifier across a range of score thresholds is generally analyzed with the help of Receiver Operating Characteristic curves, as discussed in Section 4.11.4 . The basic approach behind generating an ROC curve is to sort the predictions according to their score values and then plot the true positive rate and the false positive rate for every possible value of score threshold. Note that this approach bears some resemblance to the FDR controlling procedures described in Section 10.1.3 , where the top few ranking instances (with the lowest p-values) are labeled as positive by the classifier in order to maximize the FDR. However, in the presence of ground truth labels, we can empirically estimate measures of classification performance for different score thresholds without making use of any explicit statistical models or assumptions.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A method for comparing classifier performance using the convex hull of ROC curves was suggested by Provost and Fawcett in [ 286 ]. Bradley [ 208 ] investigated the use of area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms. Despite the vast body of literature on optimizing the AUC measure in machine learning models, it is well-known that AUC suffers from certain limitations. For example, the AUC can be used to compare the quality of two classifiers only if the ROC curve of one classifier strictly dominates the other. However, if the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect at any point, then it is difficult to assess the relative quality of classifiers using the AUC measure. An in-depth discussion of the pitfalls in using AUC as a performance measure can be obtained in works by Hand [ 245 , 246 ], and Powers [ 284 ]. The AUC has also been considered to be an incoherent measure of performance, i.e., it uses different scales while comparing the performance of different classifiers, although a coherent interpretation of AUC has been provided by Ferri et al. Berrar and Flach [ 203 ] describe some of the common caveats in using the ROC curve for clinical microarray research. An alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier is the precision-recall (PR) curve, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance [ 292 ].

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: When the score threshold is lowest (every instance is labeled as positive), the precision is equal to while recall is 1. As we increase the score threshold, the number of predicted positives can stay the same or decrease. In general, the precision may increase or decrease for the same value of recall, upon addition of an instance into the set of predicted positives. For example, if the k ranked instanceth belongs to the negative class, then including it will result in a drop in the precision without affecting the recall. The precision may improve at the next step, which adds the ranked instance, if this instance(k+1)th belongs to the positive class. Hence, the PR curve is not a smooth, monotonically increasing curve like the ROC curve, and generally has a zigzag pattern. This pattern is more prominent in the left part of the curve, where even a small change in the number of false positives can cause a large change in precision.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, axes, critical points, random classifier behavior, curve shape, and class imbalance properties of ROC Space.
The draft distinguishes ROC Space from the ROC Curve by focusing on the coordinate system and its properties rather than the specific curve generated by a single classifier.
contextual_kc_draft.text: ROC Space (TPR vs. FPR) is the two-dimensional coordinate system used to visualize the trade-off between a classifier's True Positive Rate (TPR) and False Positive Rate (FPR). In this space, the TPR is plotted along the y-axis and the FPR is plotted along the x-axis. Each point in this space represents a specific operating point of a classifier, generated by placing a particular threshold on the test scores produced by the model. The space is bounded by four critical points: (TPR=0, FPR=0) for a model that predicts every instance as negative; (TPR=1, FPR=0) for a perfect model with zero misclassifications; (TPR=1, FPR=1) for a model that predicts every instance as positive; and (TPR=0, FPR=1) for a model that predicts every instance as negative when the actual class is positive. A model that makes random guesses resides along the main diagonal connecting (TPR=0, FPR=0) and (TPR=1, FPR=1), where the TPR and FPR are equal to the fixed probability p of classifying an instance as positive. A good classification model is located as close as possible to the upper left corner of the diagram. The ROC curve within this space has a staircase pattern because the TPR monotonically increases with FPR as test instances are included in the set of predicted positives. ROC Space is agnostic to the skew in the test set because both TPR and FPR are invariant to class imbalance, making it unsuitable for measuring the impact of skew on classification performance. The space facilitates the comparison of classifiers over a range of operating points, allowing users to select a threshold based on application requirements, such as prioritizing high TPR in the early retrieval range for imbalanced test sets.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a measure used to summarize the aggregate behavior of a classifier across all operating points. It serves as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms, providing a single value that reflects overall classification quality. In terms of scale, a perfect classifier yields an AUC of 1, while an algorithm that performs random guessing results in an AUC of 0.5. A specific formulation describes the AUC as the number of correctly ranked positive-negative pairs. However, the AUC has significant limitations when used to compare classifiers. A higher AUC for one algorithm does not guarantee that it is strictly better than another, as this would require the ROC curve of the first algorithm to dominate the second across all operating points. If the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect, it is difficult to assess their relative quality using the AUC measure alone. Additionally, the AUC is considered insensitive to class skew in the test set, which contrasts with the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUC-PR), a metric that varies with skew and is often more suited for evaluating performance in the presence of class imbalance.

To summarize the aggregate behavior across all operating points, one of the commonly used measures is the area under the ROC curve (AUC). If the classifier is perfect, then its area under the ROC curve will be equal 1. If the algorithm simply performs random guessing, then its area under the ROC curve will be equal to 0.5. Although the AUC provides a useful summary of aggregate performance, there are certain caveats in using the AUC for comparing classifiers. First, even if the AUC of algorithm A is higher than the AUC of another algorithm B , this does not mean that algorithm A is always better than B , i.e., the ROC curve of A dominates that of B across all operating points. For example, even though shows a slightly lower AUC than in Figure 4.54 , we can see that both and are useful over different ranges of operating points and none of them are strictly better than the other across all possible operating points. Hence, we cannot use the AUC to determine which algorithm is better, unless we know that the ROC curve of one of the algorithms dominates the other.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A method for comparing classifier performance using the convex hull of ROC curves was suggested by Provost and Fawcett in [ 286 ]. Bradley [ 208 ] investigated the use of area under the ROC curve (AUC) as a performance metric for machine learning algorithms. Despite the vast body of literature on optimizing the AUC measure in machine learning models, it is well-known that AUC suffers from certain limitations. For example, the AUC can be used to compare the quality of two classifiers only if the ROC curve of one classifier strictly dominates the other. However, if the ROC curves of two classifiers intersect at any point, then it is difficult to assess the relative quality of classifiers using the AUC measure. An in-depth discussion of the pitfalls in using AUC as a performance measure can be obtained in works by Hand [ 245 , 246 ], and Powers [ 284 ]. The AUC has also been considered to be an incoherent measure of performance, i.e., it uses different scales while comparing the performance of different classifiers, although a coherent interpretation of AUC has been provided by Ferri et al. Berrar and Flach [ 203 ] describe some of the common caveats in using the ROC curve for clinical microarray research. An alternate approach for measuring the aggregate performance of a classifier is the precision-recall (PR) curve, which is especially useful in the presence of class imbalance [ 292 ].

contextual_kc_draft.text: The threshold effect on precision, recall, and F1 describes how changing the score threshold of a classifier alters the set of predicted positives, thereby shifting the values of precision and recall. A lower threshold results in more instances being predicted as positive. When the score threshold is at its lowest, every instance is labeled as positive, resulting in a recall of 1 and a precision equal to the overall fraction of positives in the dataset. As the score threshold increases, the number of predicted positives can stay the same or decrease. Because the precision may increase or decrease for the same value of recall upon the addition of an instance into the set of predicted positives, the precision-recall (PR) curve is not a smooth, monotonically increasing curve like the ROC curve, and generally exhibits a zigzag pattern. This pattern is more prominent in the left part of the curve, where even a small change in the number of false positives can cause a large change in precision. The PR curve plots the precision and recall values of a classifier on the y and x axes respectively, by varying the threshold on the test scores. The approach for generating a PR curve is similar to the approach described for generating an ROC curve. PR curves are sensitive to the skew factor, defined as the ratio of positives to the sum of positives and negatives, and different PR curves are generated for different values of this factor. Both precision and recall can be viewed as special cases of the F-beta measure by setting the beta parameter to 0 and infinity, respectively.
