coverage_notes: The draft covers the primary definitions of a cluster: distance-based, prototype-based, graph-based, and density-based.

The draft includes the conditions and limitations of each definition, such as the requirement for well-separated clusters in the distance-based definition and the sensitivity to noise in the contiguity-based definition.
The draft mentions the concept of conceptual clustering and its relationship to pattern recognition.
contextual_kc_draft.text:
A cluster is fundamentally defined as a set of objects in which each object is closer (or more similar) to every other object in the cluster than to any object not in the cluster. This idealistic definition is satisfied only when the data contains natural clusters that are quite far from each other, and well-separated clusters do not need to be globular but can have any shape. Sometimes a threshold is used to specify that all the objects in a cluster must be sufficiently close (or similar) to one another. 

More generally, a cluster can be defined as a set of objects that share some property. For example, objects in a center-based cluster share the property that they are all closest to the same centroid or medoid. In this context, a cluster is a set of objects in which each object is closer (more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster. For data with continuous attributes, the prototype of a cluster is often a centroid, i.e., the average (mean) of all the points in the cluster. When a centroid is not meaningful, such as when the data has categorical attributes, the prototype is often a medoid, i.e., the most representative point of a cluster. For many types of data, the prototype can be regarded as the most central point, and in such instances, we commonly refer to prototype-based clusters as center-based clusters. Not surprisingly, such clusters tend to be globular.

If the data is represented as a graph, where the nodes are objects and the links represent connections among objects, then a cluster can be defined as a connected component; i.e., a group of objects that are connected to one another, but that have no connection to objects outside the group. An important example of graph-based clusters is a contiguity-based cluster, where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other. This implies that each object in a contiguity-based cluster is closer to some other object in the cluster than to any point in a different cluster. This definition of a cluster is useful when clusters are irregular or intertwined. However, this approach can have trouble when noise is present since a small bridge of points can merge two distinct clusters.

A cluster is also defined as a dense region of objects that is surrounded by a region of low density. A density-based definition of a cluster is often employed when the clusters are irregular or intertwined, and when noise and outliers are present. By contrast, a contiguity-based definition of a cluster would not work well for data with noise because the noise would tend to form bridges between clusters.

In many applications, the notion of a cluster is not well defined. The definition of a cluster is imprecise and the best definition depends on the nature of data and the desired results. The process of finding clusters that require a very specific concept of a cluster to be successfully detected is called conceptual clustering. However, too sophisticated a notion of a cluster would take us into the area of pattern recognition, and thus, we only consider simpler types of clusters in this context.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A cluster is a dense region of objects that is surrounded by a region of low density. Figure 7.2(d) shows some density-based clusters for data created by adding noise to the data of Figure 7.2(c) . The two circular clusters are not merged, as in Figure 7.2(c) , because the bridge between them fades into the noise. Likewise, the curve that is present in Figure 7.2(c) also fades into the noise and does not form a cluster in Figure 7.2(d) . A densitybased definition of a cluster is often employed when the clusters are irregular or intertwined, and when noise and outliers are present. By contrast, a contiguity-based definition of a cluster would not work well for the data of Figure 7.2(d) because the noise would tend to form bridges between clusters.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: A cluster is a set of objects in which each object is closer (more similar) to the prototype that defines the cluster than to the prototype of any other cluster. For data with continuous attributes, the prototype of a cluster is often a centroid, i.e., the average (mean) of all the points in the cluster. When a centroid is not meaningful, such as when the data has categorical attributes, the prototype is often a medoid, i.e., the most representative point of a cluster. For many types of data, the prototype can be regarded as the most central point, and in such instances, we commonly refer to prototype-based clusters as center-based clusters . Not surprisingly, such clusters tend to be globular. Figure 7.2(b) shows an example of center-based clusters.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: If the data is represented as a graph, where the nodes are objects and the links represent connections among objects (see Section 2.1.2 ), then a cluster can be defined as a connected component ; i.e., a group of objects that are connected to one another, but that have no connection to objects outside the group. An important example of graph-based clusters is a contiguity-based cluster , where two objects are connected only if they are within a specified distance of each other. This implies that each object in a contiguity-based cluster is closer to some other object in the cluster than to any point in a different cluster. Figure 7.2(c) shows an example of such clusters for two-dimensional points. This definition of a cluster is useful when clusters are irregular or intertwined. However, this approach can have trouble when noise is present since, as illustrated by the two spherical clusters of Figure 7.2(c) , a small bridge of points can merge two distinct clusters.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: More generally, we can define a cluster as a set of objects that share some property. e.g., objects in a center-based cluster share the property that they are all closest to the same centroid or medoid. However, the shared-property approach also includes new types of clusters. A triangular area (cluster) is adjacent to a rectangular one, and there are two intertwined circles (clusters). In both cases, a clustering algorithm would need a very specific concept of a cluster to successfully detect these clusters. The process of finding such clusters is called conceptual clustering. However, too sophisticated a notion of a cluster would take us into the area of pattern recognition, and thus, we only consider simpler types of clusters in this book.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Cluster Description One aspect of clustering techniques that is often overlooked is how the resulting clusters are described. Prototype clusters are succinctly described by a small set of cluster prototypes. In the case of mixture models, the clusters are described in terms of small sets of parameters, such as the mean vector and the covariance matrix. This is also a very compact and understandable representation. For SOM, it is typically possible to visualize the relationships between clusters in a two-dimensional plot, such as that of Figure 8.8 . For graph- and density-based clustering approaches, however, clusters are typically described as sets of cluster members. Nonetheless, in CURE, clusters can be described by a (relatively) small set of representative points. Also, for grid-based clustering schemes, such as CLIQUE, more compact descriptions can be generated in terms of conditions on the attribute values that describe the grid cells in the cluster.

To better understand the difficulty of deciding what constitutes a cluster, consider Figure 7.1 , which shows 20 points and three different ways of dividing them into clusters. The shapes of the markers indicate cluster membership. However, the apparent division of each of the two larger clusters into three subclusters may simply be an artifact of the human visual system. Also, it may not be unreasonable to say that the points form four clusters, as shown in Figure 7.1(c) . This figure illustrates that the definition of a cluster is imprecise and that the best definition depends on the nature of data and the desired results.

coverage_notes: The draft synthesizes the definition of intra-cluster distance in K-means, its role in the KMI imputation procedure, and its definition in the silhouette coefficient context.
The draft explicitly contrasts intra-cluster distance with inter-cluster distance using the exclusion rule provided in the evidence.
contextual_kc_draft.text: Intra-cluster distance, also referred to as intra-cluster dissimilarity, measures the internal cohesion of a cluster by quantifying the distances between objects and the cluster's centroid. In K-means clustering, this metric is calculated as the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster to which they are assigned. The centroid represents the mean value of the objects within that cluster. The primary objective of clustering is to divide a data set into groups based on object similarity while minimizing this intra-cluster dissimilarity. In the context of K-means Clustering Imputation (KMI), the distance between a centroid and an object is denoted as d(vk, xi), where vk is the centroid of cluster k and xi is the object. The KMI procedure involves randomly selecting K complete data objects as centroids, iteratively modifying the partition to reduce the sum of distances for each object from its cluster centroid, and finally filling in non-reference attributes for incomplete objects using a nearest neighbor approach. The process terminates when the summation of distances falls below a user-specified threshold or when no changes occur to the centroids in the last iteration. In other clustering contexts, such as the silhouette coefficient, intra-cluster distance is defined as the average distance from a point to the members of its own cluster. In hierarchical clustering, within-cluster distances are explicitly excluded when computing inter-cluster distances to ensure that only cross-cluster pairs are considered for merging.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: In K-means clustering [53], the intra-cluster dissimilarity is measured by the summation of distances between the objects and the centroid of the cluster they are assigned to. A cluster centroid represents the mean value of the objects in the cluster. Given a set of objects, the overall objective of clustering is to divide the data set into groups based on the similarity of objects, and to minimize the intra-cluster dissimilarity. KMI measures the intra-cluster dissimilarity by the addition of distances among the objects and the centroid of the cluster which they are assigned to. A cluster centroid represents the mean value of the objects in the cluster. Once the clusters have converged, the last process is to fill in all the non-reference attributes for each incomplete object based on the cluster information. Data objects that belong to the same cluster are taken to be nearest neighbors of each other, and KMI applies a nearest neighbor algorithm to replace MVs, in a similar way to KNNI.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Inter-cluster distance is a measure of proximity or dissimilarity between two distinct clusters, used to determine how clusters relate to one another in hierarchical and other clustering schemes. In the CURE algorithm, the distance between two clusters is defined as the minimum distance between any two representative points, after those points have been shrunk toward their respective cluster centers. This approach is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering under specific parameter conditions and roughly the same as single-link hierarchical clustering under others. In single-link hierarchical clustering, the distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any point in one cluster and any point in the other; this distance determines the height at which the clusters are merged in a dendrogram. In silhouette coefficient evaluation, the inter-cluster component is represented by b(x), which is the smallest average distance from a point x to the members of any other cluster. BIRCH defines a number of different distance measures for clusters, all of which can be computed using summary statistics, and the diameter (variance) of the merged cluster can also be used as a distance measure. Inter-cluster distance uses only cross-cluster pairs, distinguishing it from intra-cluster distance which measures distances within the same cluster. Clustering requires a meaningful distance or similarity measure to function effectively.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Here we discuss the cophenetic correlation, a popular evaluation measure for hierarchical clusterings. The cophenetic distance between two objects is the proximity at which an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique puts the objects in the same cluster for the first time. For example, if at some point in the agglomerative hierarchical clustering process, the smallest distance between the two clusters that are merged is 0.1, then all points in one cluster have a cophenetic distance of 0.1 with respect to the points in the other cluster. In a cophenetic distance matrix, the entries are the cophenetic distances between each pair of objects. The cophenetic distance is different for each hierarchical clustering of a set of points.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The distinction between classification and clustering is defined by the source of the labels used to group objects. Classification involves assigning particular objects to pre-existing groups, a process that relies on a model developed from objects with known class labels. In contrast, clustering involves dividing objects into groups based on shared characteristics, where the groups are discovered rather than predefined. Because clustering derives its labels solely from the data itself, it is often referred to as unsupervised classification. While both processes result in a labeling of objects, the fundamental difference lies in the availability of prior knowledge: classification uses known labels to build a model for new, unlabeled objects, whereas clustering identifies potential classes without such prior guidance. This distinction is central to understanding how different data mining techniques approach the task of organizing data into meaningful groups.

The draft includes the context of how a non-compliant measure can be modified to satisfy the properties.
contextual_kc_draft.text: A distance function d(x, y) between two points x and y is characterized by three fundamental properties: positivity, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. Positivity requires that d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y, and that d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y. Symmetry requires that d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y. The triangle inequality requires that d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z. These properties define the standard behavior of distances such as the Euclidean distance. A dissimilarity measure that fails to satisfy these properties, such as a set-based distance defined as the size of the set difference A - B, can be modified to satisfy them by using the sum of the sizes of both set differences, size(A - B) + size(B - A).

The importance ofL22 Bregman divergence functions is that any such function can be used as the basis of a K-means style clustering algorithm with the mean as the centroid. Specifically, if we use a Bregman divergence as our proximity function, then the resulting clustering algorithm has the usual properties of K-means with respect to convergence, local minima, etc. Furthermore, the properties of such a clustering algorithm can be developed for all possible Bregman divergences. For example, K-means algorithms that use cosine similarity or squared Euclidean distance are particular instances of a general clustering algorithm based on Bregman divergences.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Euclidean distance is a metric distance measure used to quantify the proximity between two points in Euclidean space. It is a specific case of the Lp norm distance family and is the most commonly used proximity measure in the literature for dense, continuous data. The measure is defined by the formula d(x, y) = √((x₁ - y₁)² + (x₂ - y₂)²), where x and y are the coordinates of the two points being compared. As a distance function, Euclidean distance satisfies the standard metric properties: positivity (d(x, y) ≥ 0 for all x and y), identity of indiscernibles (d(x, y) = 0 only if x = y), symmetry (d(x, y) = d(y, x) for all x and y), and the triangle inequality (d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z) for all points x, y, and z). In practice, Euclidean distance is frequently employed in clustering algorithms such as K-means, where it serves as the basis for calculating the sum of squared errors (SSE) to evaluate cluster quality. It is also used in imputation methods like K-Nearest Neighbour (KNN) to identify the closest instances for estimating missing values. While Euclidean distance compares the absolute locations of points, it is distinct from similarity measures like cosine similarity, which compares direction or pattern, and from other distance metrics like Manhattan distance, which measures distance by moving step-by-step along the axes.

For our objective function, which measures the quality of a clustering, we use the sum of the squared error (SSE) , which is also known as scatter. evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The last entry in the table, Bregman divergence (Section 2.4.8 ), is actually a class of proximity measures that includes the squared Euclidean distance, , the Mahalanobis distance, and cosine similarity. The importance ofL22 Bregman divergence functions is that any such function can be used as the basis of a K-means style clustering algorithm with the mean as the centroid. Specifically, if we use a Bregman divergence as our proximity function, then the resulting clustering algorithm has the usual properties of K-means with respect to convergence, local minima, etc. Furthermore, the properties of such a clustering algorithm can be developed for all possible Bregman divergences. For example, K-means algorithms that use cosine similarity or squared Euclidean distance are particular instances of a general clustering algorithm based on Bregman divergences.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Manhattan distance is a distance measure that quantifies the separation between two points by summing the absolute differences of their coordinates, effectively measuring the distance if one moves step by step along the axes, like walking through city blocks. Formally, for two points x and y with m dimensions, the Manhattan distance is defined as d_Manhattan(x, y) = Σ_{i=1}^{m} |x_i - y_i|. This measure is bounded such that 0 ≤ d_Manhattan(x, y) < ∞. In the context of clustering, when the objective is to minimize the sum of the distances, the appropriate centroid for a cluster using Manhattan distance is the median of the points in that cluster. This distinguishes it from similarity scores, where larger values indicate greater similarity, and from Euclidean distance, which is calculated using the square root of the sum of squared differences.

common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing Manhattan distance with Euclidean distance (sum of squares vs sum of absolute values).
Confusing distance metrics with similarity scores regarding the direction of the value (minimization vs maximization).
Using the mean instead of the median as the centroid when minimizing Manhattan distance.

Claiming that the mean is the optimal centroid for minimizing Manhattan distance.
Omitting the absolute value in the formula when describing the calculation.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
Cosine similarity is a similarity score used to measure the relationship between two data objects, such as documents represented as vectors. Unlike distance measures such as Manhattan or Euclidean distance, which quantify how far apart two points are, cosine similarity quantifies how similar two objects are, with larger values indicating greater similarity. It is defined as the cosine of the angle between the two vectors. When the cosine similarity is 1, the angle between the vectors is 0 degrees, meaning they point in the same direction and are identical except for length. When the cosine similarity is 0, the angle is 90 degrees, indicating the vectors are perpendicular and do not share any terms. When the cosine similarity is -1, the vectors point in exactly opposite directions.

The calculation involves normalizing the vectors by dividing each by its length, resulting in unit vectors. For unit vectors, the cosine similarity can be calculated as a simple inner product. This normalization means that cosine similarity does not take the length of the data objects into account, making it particularly useful for sparse data such as documents where the magnitude of the vector (e.g., document length) may not be relevant to the similarity of content. In contrast, Euclidean distance compares locations and is sensitive to length, making it more appropriate for dense data or when magnitude is important. Cosine similarity is often used in clustering algorithms, such as K-means variants, to maximize the cohesion of clusters by maximizing the similarity of objects to the cluster centroid.

common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing cosine similarity with Euclidean distance, especially regarding how they handle vector magnitude.
Assuming that a cosine similarity of 0 means the vectors are identical or that the vectors are zero vectors.
Misinterpreting the sign of cosine similarity in contexts where vectors are non-negative (like document term frequencies), where -1 is not possible.

Why cosine similarity is invariant to vector length and why this is beneficial for sparse data like documents.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The last entry in the table, Bregman divergence ( Section 2.4.8 ), is actually a class of proximity measures that includes the squared Euclidean distance, , the Mahalanobis distance, and cosine similarity. The importance of Bregman divergence functions is that any such function can be used as the basis of a K-means style clustering algorithm with the mean as the centroid. Specifically, if we use a Bregman divergence as our proximity function, then the resulting clustering algorithm has the usual properties of K-means with respect to convergence, local minima, etc. Furthermore, the properties of such a clustering algorithm can be developed for all possible Bregman divergences. For example, K-means algorithms that use cosine similarity or squared Euclidean distance are particular instances of a general clustering algorithm based on Bregman divergences.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The Rand Index is an external validation measure used to evaluate clustering by comparing the cluster structure against true class labels. It is a similarity-oriented measure that operates by comparing pairs of distinct objects, meaning it does not require the original feature values once cluster assignments and class labels are available. The index is calculated using the formula: Rand Index = (f11 + f00) / (f11 + f10 + f01 + f00). In this formula, f11 represents pairs of objects that are in the same cluster and belong to the same class, while f00 represents pairs that are in different clusters and belong to different classes. The denominator represents the total number of pairs of distinct objects. The Rand Index specifically includes f00, the pairs that are correctly separated in both the class structure and the clustering. This distinguishes it from the Jaccard Coefficient, which ignores f00 and focuses only on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. Because the Rand Index includes f00, it is often higher than the Jaccard Coefficient. The measure can be computed through class similarity and cluster similarity matrices, where diagonal elements (representing objects compared to themselves) are not counted because only pairs of distinct objects are considered. In some contexts, the adjusted Rand index is used, which is based on the multivariate hypergeometric distribution to allow for the computation of p-values.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The Jaccard coefficient is a similarity measure used to quantify the similarity between two binary vectors, particularly in contexts involving asymmetric binary attributes such as transaction data where a value of 1 indicates the presence of an item and 0 indicates its absence. It is frequently employed as a cluster validity measure and is often symbolized by j. The coefficient is defined by the formula Jaccard coefficient = f11 / (f11 + f10 + f01), where f11 represents the number of attributes where both objects have a 1, f10 represents the number of attributes where the first object has a 1 and the second has a 0, and f01 represents the number of attributes where the first object has a 0 and the second has a 1. A key characteristic of this measure is that it ignores f00, the count of attributes where both objects have a 0, focusing exclusively on pairs that are together in at least one of the two structures. This distinguishes it from other similarity measures like the Simple Matching Coefficient (Rand statistic), which includes f00 in its calculation. For example, given f00=4, f01=2, f10=2, and f11=2, the Jaccard coefficient is calculated as 2 / (2 + 2 + 2) = 0.33. The measure can also be extended to more than two variables using multidimensional contingency tables, and an extended version exists for document data that reduces to the standard Jaccard coefficient for binary attributes.

The draft excludes specific formulas for weighted similarity (e.g., similarity(x,y) = sum(wk*delta_k*sk)/sum(wk*delta_k)) as these are general similarity function definitions rather than specific to the matrix structure itself, though they are used to populate the matrix.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
A similarity matrix is a square matrix that stores the pairwise similarity between every pair of objects in a data set. The similarity between two objects is a numerical measure of the degree to which they are alike; higher values indicate greater similarity. Similarities are usually nonnegative and are often scaled to the interval [0, 1], where 0 represents no similarity and 1 represents complete similarity. To facilitate comparison, similarity values are frequently transformed to this standard range using a linear transformation such as s' = (s - min_s) / (max_s - min_s), where s is the original similarity value, and min_s and max_s are the minimum and maximum similarity values in the data set. This transformation preserves the relative distances between points.

In the context of clustering, the similarity matrix is used to evaluate the 'goodness' of a clustering by comparing it against an ideal cluster similarity matrix. An ideal cluster similarity matrix is constructed by assigning a value of 1 to an entry if the associated pair of points belongs to the same cluster, and 0 otherwise. When the rows and columns of the matrix are sorted so that objects belonging to the same cluster are grouped together, this ideal matrix exhibits a block diagonal structure, with non-zero values inside the blocks representing intra-cluster similarity and zero values elsewhere. The correlation between the actual similarity matrix and this ideal matrix serves as a measure of cluster validity, a metric known as Hubert's Γ statistic.

The similarity matrix can also be used for visual inspection of clustering results. By ordering the matrix with respect to cluster labels and plotting it, the patterns displayed can reveal the relationships between clusters. For instance, well-separated clusters are illustrated by a reordered similarity matrix where high similarity values are concentrated within cluster blocks. Additionally, in centroid-based clustering, the pairwise similarity or distance of the centroids can be computed to provide a more comprehensive view of cluster cohesion and separation. This approach is analogous to examining a confusion matrix in classification problems rather than relying solely on aggregate measures like accuracy or the F-measure.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a visual example of a reordered similarity matrix to show well-separated clusters.
Demonstrating the linear transformation formula to scale similarity values.
Comparing the actual similarity matrix to the ideal binary matrix to explain Hubert's Γ statistic.
Explaining how the matrix provides a more comprehensive view than single aggregate metrics.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the similarity matrix with a confusion matrix used in classification.
Assuming the similarity matrix only contains binary values, when it can contain continuous similarity scores.
Failing to sort the matrix by cluster labels before interpreting the block diagonal structure.
Confusing the similarity matrix with a specific similarity metric like Cosine Similarity.
red_flags: Stating that the similarity matrix is only used for classification.
Claiming that the ideal similarity matrix has non-zero values outside the cluster blocks.
Omitting the definition of the ideal matrix when discussing correlation-based validation.
Confusing the diagonal entries (self-similarity) with off-diagonal entries (pairwise similarity) in the context of validity measures.
what_tutor_should_explain: The definition of a similarity matrix as a pairwise representation of object similarity.
The construction of the ideal cluster similarity matrix with 1s for same-cluster pairs and 0s otherwise.
The block diagonal structure of the ideal matrix when sorted by cluster labels.
The use of correlation between actual and ideal matrices as a validity measure (Hubert's Γ).
The linear transformation of similarity values to the [0, 1] interval.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, centroid formula, iterative procedure, and key characteristics (centroid-based, initialization sensitivity, complexity) supported by the evidence.
Evidence regarding Bisecting K-Means was excluded as it belongs to a sibling unit.
contextual_kc_draft.text:
K-Means is a partitional clustering algorithm that directly divides data into K clusters, where K is a user-specified parameter representing the desired number of clusters. Each cluster is represented by a centroid, which is the representative centre of the cluster. For Euclidean K-Means, the centroid is defined as the mean of all points in the cluster; specifically, if a cluster C_i contains m_i points, the centroid c_i is calculated as the sum of the points in C_i divided by m_i. A centroid is a mean position and does not have to be one of the original data points.

The algorithm operates through an iterative procedure. First, K initial centroids are chosen. Next, each point is assigned to the closest centroid, forming the clusters. Then, each centroid is recomputed as the mean of the points assigned to it. This cycle of assignment and centroid update is repeated until the assignments stop changing or the centroids remain the same.

K-Means is a centroid-based algorithm, and its performance is often evaluated using centroid-based cohesion and separation measures. The algorithm is simple but can be sensitive to initialization; random initialization is often used, which may result in a clustering that represents a local minimum in terms of the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE). While there are choices for the proximity function, centroid, and objective function that guarantee convergence, the basic algorithm's efficiency can be impacted when K is large, as the distance of each point to each cluster centroid must be calculated at each iteration.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a simple 2D example to demonstrate the assignment and update steps.
Explaining why random initialization can lead to different results.
Contrasting K-Means with Bisecting K-Means to highlight the partitional vs. hierarchical distinction.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing K-Means with Bisecting K-Means, which is a hierarchical variant.
Assuming centroids must be original data points (they are means and can be between points).
Believing K-Means always finds the global optimum (it can get stuck in local minima due to initialization).
Confusing the partitional nature of K-Means with the hierarchical nature of other clustering methods.
red_flags: Stating that K-Means produces a hierarchy of clusters.
Claiming that the centroid is always one of the input data points.
Suggesting that K-Means does not require a pre-specified number of clusters K.
what_tutor_should_explain: The iterative nature of the algorithm: assignment followed by centroid update.
The definition of a centroid as the mean of the points in the cluster.
The role of the parameter K as the user-specified number of clusters.
The convergence condition: stopping when assignments or centroids stop changing.

contextual_kc_draft.text: The SSE Optimization Criterion is an objective function used in clustering that seeks to minimize the total squared error (SSE). When applied to clustering, this criterion frames the task as an optimization problem where the goal is to find a partition of points that minimizes the total SSE. Because the general clustering problem for this objective is computationally infeasible to solve exhaustively, practical algorithms use local optimization strategies. For instance, agglomerative hierarchical clustering uses the criterion to make local decisions about which clusters to merge at each step, avoiding the need to solve the hard global combinatorial optimization problem. In Ward’s method, the “minimize squared error” criterion guides the merging of clusters, although the resulting clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE and may not be stable. This local optimization approach is often used to initialize K-means clustering, indicating a connection between local and global “minimize squared error” objectives. The criterion distinguishes between global minima, which represent the best possible clustering, and local minima, which are suboptimal solutions that satisfy the objective function only within a limited region of the solution space.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms tend to make good local decisions about combining two clusters because they can use information about the pairwise similarity of all points. However, once a decision is made to merge two clusters, it cannot be undone at a later time. This approach prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global optimization criterion. For example, although the “minimize squared error” criterion from Kmeans is used in deciding which clusters to merge in Ward’s method, the clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE. Indeed, the clusters are not even stable, in the sense that a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of some other cluster than it is to the centroid of its current cluster. Nonetheless, Ward’s method is often used as a robust method of initializing a K-means clustering, indicating that a local “minimize squared error” objective function does have a connection to a global “minimize squared error” objective function.

contextual_kc_draft.text: K-Means Complexity refers to the computational resource requirements of the K-means clustering algorithm, specifically its time and space complexity. The space requirements for K-means are modest because the algorithm stores only the data points and centroids. The storage required is O((m+K)n), where m is the number of data points, K is the number of clusters, and n is the number of attributes. The time requirements for K-means are also modest and are basically linear in the number of data points. The time required is O(I×K×m×n), where I is the number of iterations required for convergence. Consequently, K-means is linear in m, the number of points, and is considered efficient and simple provided that K, the number of clusters, is significantly less than m. The algorithm's complexity is analyzed by considering each step of the basic K-means algorithm in detail. While the evidence notes that K-means has a time complexity, it does not provide a specific value for comparison with DBSCAN, nor does it provide the specific time and space complexity values for fuzzy c-means to allow for a direct comparison.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Centroid Initialization Sensitivity describes the dependence of K-means clustering results on the selection of initial centroids. Standard K-means is susceptible to initialization problems, which can be mitigated by using variants like bisecting K-means or by applying postprocessing to fix the resulting clusters. Bisecting K-means is less susceptible to these issues because it performs several trial bisections and selects the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), and because it operates with only two centroids at each step. An alternative initialization strategy involves selecting the first point at random or as the centroid of all points, then iteratively selecting the point farthest from any already-selected initial centroid. This approach guarantees well-separated centroids but can select outliers rather than points in dense regions, potentially leading to clusters with only one point. To address this, the farthest-point approach is often applied to a sample of points, as outliers are rare and less likely to appear in a random sample, while points from dense regions are likely to be included. K-means++ is another approach that picks centroids incrementally; at each step, each point has a probability of being picked as the new centroid proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid. This method is guaranteed to find a solution optimal to within a factor of O(log(k)), translating to noticeably better clustering results in terms of lower SSE. In a specific example, bisecting K-means was executed with K=3 leaf clusters using Euclidean distance, assigning objects to clusters, computing SSE, and finding centroids in each iteration, with initial centroids p10 and p11.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: More recently, a new approach for initializing K-means, called K-means++, has been developed. This procedure is guaranteed to find a K-means clustering solution that is optimal to within a factor of , which inO log(k) practice translates into noticeably better clustering results in terms of lower SSE. This technique is similar to the idea just discussed of picking the first centroid at random and then picking each remaining centroid as the point as far from the remaining centroids as possible. Specifically, K-means++ picks centroids incrementally until k centroids have been picked. At every such step, each point has a probability of being picked as the new centroid that is proportional to the square of its distance to its closest centroid. It might seem that this approach might tend to choose outliers for centroids, but because outliers are rare, by definition, this is unlikely.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: The following procedure is another approach to selecting initial centroids. Select the first point at random or take the centroid of all points. Then, for each successive initial centroid, select the point that is farthest from any of the initial centroids already selected. In this way, we obtain a set of initial centroids that is guaranteed to be not only randomly selected but also well separated. Unfortunately, such an approach can select outliers, rather than points in dense regions (clusters), which can lead to a situation where many clusters have just one point-an outlier-which reduces the number of centroids for forming clusters for the majority of points. Also, it is expensive to compute the farthest point from the current set of initial centroids. To overcome these problems, this approach is often applied to a sample of the points. Because outliers are rare, they tend not to show up in a random sample. In contrast, points from every dense region are likely to be included unless the sample size is very small. Also, the computation involved in finding the initial centroids is greatly reduced because the sample size is typically much smaller than the number of points.

contextual_kc_draft.text: K-Means and its variations have specific limitations regarding the types of clusters they can detect. The algorithm requires a meaningful distance metric and a meaningful mean; consequently, it cannot be applied to raw categories because such data do not have meaningful averages. Traditional K-Means is sensitive to outliers and has difficulty handling clusters that differ significantly in size or density, or that possess non-globular shapes. When clusters have non-spherical shapes or widely different sizes or densities, K-Means struggles to identify the natural groupings. For instance, if one cluster is much larger than others, the larger cluster may be broken while a smaller cluster is combined with a portion of the larger one. Similarly, if smaller clusters are much denser than a larger cluster, the algorithm fails to find the natural clusters. In cases where the natural clusters are not globular, K-Means may produce clusters that mix portions of the natural groups. Additionally, the algorithm is subject to convergence issues where it reaches a local minimum, meaning it cannot improve from its current path, rather than finding the global minimum where no possible clustering with the same K has a lower total SSE.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Bisecting K-Means is a hierarchical clustering algorithm that extends the basic K-Means method by constructing a hierarchy of clusters through a sequence of binary splits. Unlike standard K-Means, which initializes K centroids simultaneously and jointly updates them, Bisecting K-Means starts with a single cluster containing all data points. The algorithm repeatedly selects one existing cluster and splits it into two subclusters using basic K-Means with K = 2. This process continues until the desired number of leaf clusters is reached. A key characteristic of this approach is that it performs several trial bisections for each split and retains the one with the lowest Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), which makes it less susceptible to initialization problems compared to standard K-Means. Additionally, because each split only requires computing distances to two centroids for a subset of points, Bisecting K-Means can run significantly faster than regular K-Means, particularly when the number of clusters is large. The algorithm produces a hierarchical structure; if a flat clustering with lower total SSE is required, the final centroids from the bisecting process can be used as initial centroids for a subsequent standard K-Means refinement step. However, if the goal is to preserve the hierarchical structure, the process stops after the final split.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, visual structure, height semantics, extraction of K clusters, and drawing conventions.
The draft distinguishes the dendrogram from the linkage methods used to compute the distances.
contextual_kc_draft.text: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram used to display the results of hierarchical clustering. It visualizes both the cluster-subcluster relationships and the order in which clusters were merged (in an agglomerative view) or split (in a divisive view). In the diagram, the vertical height at which two clusters are joined reflects the distance between those clusters; for example, if the distance between two points is 0.11, they are joined at a height of 0.11. The root of the dendrogram is at level 1, and the diagram can be used to extract a flat clustering of K clusters by taking the clusters at the K-th level. When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing of the leaves does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and the nested structure are essential. The leaf order must match the nested structure exactly, although branches can be flipped left-to-right. The dendrogram is distinct from the linkage criteria (such as single link, complete link, or group average) that determine the distances used to build the hierarchy.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a worked example to show how distance values map to merge heights.
Demonstrating how to flip branches left-to-right without changing the meaning of the dendrogram.
Comparing the dendrogram to a nested cluster diagram for 2D data.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing the dendrogram with the linkage method used to build it.
Believing that the horizontal spacing in a dendrogram carries semantic meaning (it does not).
Failing to recognize that the root is at level 1 when extracting K clusters.
Assuming that hierarchical clustering avoids choosing K entirely (it avoids choosing it before building, but a cut is still needed for a flat result).
red_flags: A student who thinks the dendrogram is a type of clustering algorithm rather than a visualization.
A student who cannot explain what the height of a merge represents.
A student who believes the horizontal position of leaves is significant.
what_tutor_should_explain: The meaning of the vertical height in a dendrogram (distance between clusters).
How to extract a flat clustering of K clusters by cutting the dendrogram at a specific level.
The importance of the nested structure and leaf order in a hand-drawn dendrogram.
That the dendrogram represents the order of merges/splits, not just the final clusters.

evidence_map.claim: A dendrogram is a tree-like diagram displaying cluster-subcluster relationships and the order of merges or splits.
The height at which two clusters are merged in a dendrogram reflects the distance between those clusters.
K clusters can be extracted from a dendrogram by taking the clusters at the K-th level, where the root is at level 1.
When drawing a dendrogram by hand, the exact horizontal spacing does not matter, but the vertical merge heights and nested structure do.
The leaf order in a dendrogram must match the nested structure exactly, but branches can be flipped left-to-right.
Hierarchical clustering avoids choosing K before building the dendrogram, but a cut is still needed to get a final flat clustering.

do_not_confuse_with: Nested cluster diagrams (an alternative visualization for 2D points, not the tree structure itself)
The specific linkage criteria (e.g., MAX, MIN, Group Average) which are inputs to the hierarchy, not the diagram itself

What does the height of a dendrogram branch mean?
How do I get K clusters from a dendrogram?

sibling_contrast_notes: Distinguish from Agglomerative Clustering: The dendrogram is the visualization of the result, while agglomerative clustering is the algorithm that builds it.
Distinguish from Linkage Methods (Single, Complete, Group Average): Linkage methods define how distances are calculated; the dendrogram displays the resulting hierarchy.
Distinguish from K-means: K-means produces a flat clustering directly, whereas hierarchical clustering produces a dendrogram from which a flat clustering can be derived.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, the distinction from divisive clustering, the core procedure (merging closest clusters), the single linkage formula, and the role of linkage methods (including Ward's and centroid).
The draft includes limitations regarding large datasets and error compounding.

The draft does not include the full CURE algorithm details as CURE is a specific application/variant rather than the core definition of agglomerative clustering itself, though it notes CURE uses an agglomerative scheme.
contextual_kc_draft.text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering is a bottom-up method that starts with every object as its own cluster and repeatedly merges the two closest clusters until one large cluster remains or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is a collection of closely related clustering techniques that produce a hierarchical clustering; some have a natural interpretation in terms of graph-based clustering, while others have an interpretation in terms of a prototype-based approach. The process is distinct from divisive clustering, which splits clusters downward, whereas agglomerative clustering merges clusters upward. A key component of this method is the linkage criterion, which determines how the distance between two clusters is calculated. For example, single linkage defines the distance between two clusters as the minimum distance between any two points in the clusters, expressed as d_single(C_i, C_j) = min_{x∈C_i, y∈C_j} d(x, y), where C_i and C_j are the two clusters and d(x, y) is the distance between points x and y. Other linkage methods include complete linkage (farthest pair), average linkage (all cross-pairs), centroid linkage (centers), and Ward's method, which is described as greedy bottom-up clustering using the K-means SSE objective. The choice of linkage method is critical because using only one approach can lead to mistakes in merging clusters; for instance, using closeness (single link) might merge clusters that almost touch instead of clusters that are intuitively more similar based on connection strength. Agglomerative clustering is often selected for global clustering tasks because it can be applied to summary information stored in clustering features. However, it has limitations: if the data is very large, it may not be directly applicable, and it can compound errors if objects are wrongly put together in a prior partitioning step, as it can never separate objects that have been merged.

acceptable_teaching_moves: Using a small dataset to demonstrate the step-by-step merging process.
Comparing the results of single linkage vs complete linkage on the same data.
Explaining Ward's method as minimizing the increase in total SSE.
Discussing the trade-offs between different linkage methods.
common_confusions_or_errors: Confusing agglomerative clustering with divisive clustering.
Assuming all agglomerative methods use the same distance metric (they use different linkage criteria).
Believing agglomerative clustering is always suitable for very large datasets (it can be computationally expensive or memory-intensive).
Thinking that the choice of linkage method does not affect the final cluster structure.
red_flags: Stating that agglomerative clustering starts with one large cluster and splits it (this is divisive).
Claiming that agglomerative clustering can 'unmerge' clusters if a mistake is made (it cannot).
Ignoring the role of the linkage criterion in determining which clusters to merge.
what_tutor_should_explain: The core mechanism: starting with singletons and merging the two closest clusters.
The role of linkage criteria (single, complete, average, centroid, Ward's) in defining 'closest'.
The difference between agglomerative (merging) and divisive (splitting) approaches.
The limitation that agglomerative clustering cannot separate objects once they are merged.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. For example, a representative point that was a distance of 10 units from the center would move by 3 units (for ), while a representative point at a distance of 1 unit would only move 0.3 units. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. The distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any two representative points (after they are shrunk toward their respective centers). While this scheme is not exactly like any other hierarchical scheme that we have seen, it is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering if , and roughly the same as single link hierarchical clustering if . Notice that while a hierarchical clustering scheme is used, the goal of CURE is to find a given number of clusters as specified by the user. CURE takes advantage of certain characteristics of the hierarchical clustering process to eliminate outliers at two different points in the clustering process. First, if a cluster is growing slowly, then it may consist of outliers, since by definition, outliers are far from others and will not be merged with other points very often. In CURE, this first phase of outlier elimination typically occurs when the number of clusters is 1/3 the original number of points. The second of K , the number of desired clusters. At this point, small clusters are again α=0.7 α=0 α=1

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: We reiterate, however, that this factor often plays an important role in determining the type of clustering algorithm to be used. Suppose that we want to create a hierarchical clustering of a set of data, we are not interested in a complete hierarchy that extends all the way to individual objects, but only to the point at which we have split the data into a few hundred clusters. If the data is very large, we cannot directly apply an agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique. We could, however, use a divisive clustering technique, such as the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which is the divisive analog to single link, but this would only work if the data set is not too large. Bisecting K- means would also work for many data sets, but if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory, then this scheme also runs into problems. In this situation, a technique such as BIRCH, which does not require that all data be in main memory, becomes more useful.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering techniques operate by merging the two most similar clusters, where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. Although there are two basic approaches, using only one of these two approaches can lead to mistakes in merging clusters. If we use the closeness of clusters (as measured by the closest two points in different clusters) as our merging criterion, then we would merge the two circular clusters, (c) and (d),which almost touch, instead of the rectangular clusters, (a) and (b), which are separated by a small gap. However, intuitively, we should have merged rectangular clusters, (a) and (b). Exercise 15 on page 700 asks for an example of a situation in which the strength of connections likewise leads to an unintuitive result.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Divisive hierarchical clustering is a top-down method that begins with all objects in a single cluster and repeatedly splits clusters into smaller clusters until singleton clusters or a stopping rule is reached. This approach is distinguished from agglomerative clustering, which merges clusters upward, by its downward splitting mechanism. Divisive clustering can be useful if the top-level split is meaningful or if a good splitter is available. Specific divisive techniques include the minimum spanning tree (MST) algorithm, which starts with the minimum spanning tree of the proximity graph and can be viewed as an application of sparsification for finding clusters; this algorithm produces the same clustering as single link agglomerative clustering. Bisecting K-means is another divisive technique that works for many data sets, though it runs into problems if the data set is large enough that it cannot be contained completely in memory. In such large-scale scenarios, techniques such as BIRCH, which do not require that all data be in main memory, become more useful. The choice of algorithm often depends on data size and memory constraints, with divisive methods like MST serving as the divisive analog to single link agglomerative clustering.

contextual_kc_draft.text: MIN (Single Linkage) is a linkage criterion used in hierarchical clustering to define the proximity between two clusters. The proximity is defined as the minimum of the distance (or the maximum of the similarity) between any two points located in the two different clusters. Formally, the distance between two clusters Ci and Cj is calculated as dsingle(Ci, Cj) = min d(x, y), where the minimum is taken over all pairs of points x in Ci and y in Cj. In this formula, d(x, y) represents the distance between individual points x and y. Conceptually, single linkage treats two clusters as close if at least one point in one cluster is close to at least one point in the other cluster, often described as using the 'nearest bridge' between the groups. Using graph terminology, the process can be viewed as starting with all points as singleton clusters and adding links between points one at a time, shortest links first, which combines the points into clusters. In terms of implementation, single linkage allows for the use of a precomputed distance matrix; the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using the minimum value. The technique is noted for being good at handling non-elliptical shapes, but it is sensitive to noise and outliers.

coverage_notes: The draft covers the definition, graph-theoretic interpretation, contrast with other linkage methods, properties (noise/outlier susceptibility, cluster shape), and the update procedure.
Specific worked examples from the evidence are included to illustrate the max operation.
contextual_kc_draft.text: MAX (Complete Linkage) is a version of hierarchical clustering in which the proximity of two clusters is defined as the maximum of the distance (or the minimum of the similarity) between any two points in the two different clusters. In graph terminology, if one starts with all points as singleton clusters and adds links between points one at a time, shortest links first, a group of points is not considered a cluster until all the points in it are completely linked, i.e., form a clique. Complete linkage says two clusters are close only if even the farthest cross-cluster pair is not too far. This contrasts with single linkage, which uses the nearest bridge, and average linkage, which averages every cross-pair distance. Complete link is less susceptible to noise and outliers, but it can break large clusters and it favors globular shapes. For single and complete linkage, the original point-distance matrix is computed once, and after a merge, the current matrix is updated using min or max. For example, the complete linkage distance between clusters {A, B} and C is calculated as the maximum of the individual distances, such as max(2, 1) = 2. Similarly, the distance between {A, B, C, D} and E is the maximum of their pairwise distances, such as max(4, 3, 2, 1) = 4. Another example shows dist({3,6}, {2,5}) = max(dist(3,2), dist(6,2), dist(3,5), dist(6,5)) = max(0.15, 0.25, 0.28, 0.39) = 0.39.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Group Average Linkage is a graph-based agglomerative clustering technique that defines the proximity between two clusters as the average of the pairwise proximities (or average length of edges) of all pairs of points from different clusters. This approach bases its notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters, such as the pairwise similarity of points, rather than relying solely on the closeness of the clusters measured by the minimum distance between points. In a full agglomerative clustering run, the distance between two specified clusters is calculated as one candidate distance, which must be compared with all other current cluster-pair distances before choosing a merge. The weighted version of group average, known as WPGMA, uses coefficients that are constants independent of cluster sizes, specifically alpha_A = 1/2, alpha_B = 1/2, beta = 0, and gamma = 0. General unweighted approaches are preferred unless there is reason to believe that individual points should have different weights. For clustering approaches like group average, outliers are potentially less problematic because they tend to form singleton or small clusters that do not merge with other clusters until much later in the merging process, allowing them to be removed by discarding these small clusters.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering techniques operate by merging the two most similar clusters, where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm. Some agglomerative algorithms, such as group average, base their notion of similarity on the strength of the connections between the two clusters (e.g., the pairwise similarity of points in the two clusters), while other techniques, such as the single link method, use the closeness of the clusters (e.g., the minimum distance between points in different clusters) to measure cluster similarity. Although there are two basic approaches, using only one of these two approaches can lead to mistakes in merging clusters. If we use the closeness of clusters (as measured by the closest two points in different clusters) as our merging criterion, then we would merge the two circular clusters, (c) and (d),which almost touch, instead of the rectangular clusters, (a) and (b), which are separated by a small gap. However, intuitively, we should have merged rectangular clusters, (a) and (b). evidence_for_synthesis.text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering techniques operate by merging the two most similar clusters, where the definition of cluster similarity depends on the particular algorithm. contextual_kc_draft.text: Ward's method is a greedy bottom-up hierarchical clustering technique that uses the same objective function as K-means clustering: minimizing the sum of squared errors (SSE). In this approach, each cluster is represented by its centroid, and the proximity between two clusters is defined as the increase in the total SSE that results from merging them. The algorithm builds a hierarchy by repeatedly evaluating all possible merges, computing the new total SSE for each candidate, and selecting the merge that causes the smallest increase in SSE. The SSE for a cluster C is calculated as the sum of the squared distances of its points from the cluster centroid μ_C: SSE(C) = Σ ||x - μ_C||². The total SSE is the sum of the SSEs of all clusters: SSE_total = SSE(C₁) + SSE(C₂) + ... + SSE(C_k). Ward's method is distinct from centroid linkage, which compares center-to-center distances, and from other linkage methods like single, complete, or average linkage. It is often used as a robust method for initializing K-means clustering, as it connects a local 'minimize squared error' objective to a global one. Outliers pose a serious problem for Ward's method because they increase SSE and distort centroids, unlike in single or complete linkage where outliers may form stable singleton clusters. Mathematically, Ward's method is very similar to the group average method when the proximity between two points is defined as the square of the distance between them.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms tend to make good local decisions about combining two clusters because they can use information about the pairwise similarity of all points. However, once a decision is made to merge two clusters, it cannot be undone at a later time. This approach prevents a local optimization criterion from becoming a global optimization criterion. For example, although the 'minimize squared error' criterion from Kmeans is used in deciding which clusters to merge in Ward's method, the clusters at each level do not represent local minima with respect to the total SSE. Indeed, the clusters are not even stable, in the sense that a point in one cluster can be closer to the centroid of some other cluster than it is to the centroid of its current cluster. Nonetheless, Ward's method is often used as a robust method of initializing a K-means clustering, indicating that a local 'minimize squared error' objective function does have a connection to a global 'minimize squared error' objective function.

contextual_kc_draft.text: Hierarchical clustering complexity refers to the computational and storage requirements of agglomerative hierarchical clustering algorithms, which are defined by their use of a proximity matrix and iterative cluster merging. The space complexity is O(m²), where m is the number of data points, because the algorithm must store the proximities between all pairs of points (assuming a symmetric matrix) and track the state of the clusters. The time complexity is O(m² log m) when using a sorted list or heap to optimize the search for the two closest clusters; without such optimization, the time complexity is O(m³). These high complexity requirements severely limit the size of data sets that can be processed directly, making the algorithm impractical for large-scale applications. The complexity arises from the need to perform m-1 iterations, where each iteration involves finding the closest clusters and updating the proximity matrix. While hierarchical clustering avoids the difficulty of solving hard combinatorial optimization problems and does not require choosing initial points, its computational cost is a significant drawback compared to scalable alternatives like bisecting K-means.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: CURE (Clustering Using REpresentatives) is a clustering algorithm that uses a variety of different techniques to create an approach that can handle large data sets, outliers, and clusters with non-spherical shapes and non-uniform sizes. CURE represents a cluster by using multiple representative points from the cluster. These points will, in theory, capture the geometry and shape of the cluster. The first representative point is chosen to be the point farthest from the center of the cluster, while the remaining points are chosen so that they are farthest from all the previously chosen points. In this way, the representative points are naturally relatively well distributed. The number of points chosen is a parameter, but it was found that a value of 10 or more worked well. Once the representative points are chosen, they are shrunk toward the center by a factor, α . This helps moderate the effect of outliers, which are usually farther away from the center and thus, are shrunk more. For example, a representative point that was a distance of 10 units from the center would move by 3 units (for ), while a representative point at a distance of 1 unit would only move 0.3 units. CURE uses an agglomerative hierarchical scheme to perform the actual clustering. The distance between two clusters is the minimum distance between any two representative points (after they are shrunk toward their respective centers). While this scheme is not exactly like any other hierarchical scheme that we have seen, it is equivalent to centroid-based hierarchical clustering if , and roughly the same as single link hierarchical clustering if . Notice that while a hierarchical clustering scheme is used, the goal of CURE is to find a given number of clusters as specified by the user. CURE takes advantage of certain characteristics of the hierarchical clustering process to eliminate outliers at two different points in the clustering process. First, if a cluster is growing slowly, then it may consist of outliers, since by definition, outliers are far from others and will not be merged with other points very often. In CURE, this first phase of outlier elimination typically occurs when the number of clusters is 1/3 the original number of points. The second of K , the number of desired clusters. The draft includes the formal condition for a core point and its role in the DBSCAN algorithm.
contextual_kc_draft.text: A core point is a data point located in the interior of a density-based cluster. Formally, a point is a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps, where MinPts and Eps are user-specified parameters. The count of points in the neighborhood includes the point itself. In density-based clustering algorithms like DBSCAN and SNN density-based clustering, core points strongly belong to one cluster and serve as the foundation for cluster construction. A core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. In the DBSCAN algorithm, any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster. Core points are distinguished from border points, which are not core but fall within the neighborhood of a core point, and from noise points, which are neither core nor border.

The evidence does not provide a formal mathematical formula for the border point condition, only descriptive definitions.
contextual_kc_draft.text: A border point is a data point that is not a core point because it does not have enough points in its neighborhood to satisfy the core point condition, but it falls within the neighborhood of at least one core point. In the context of density-based clustering, a border point is located on the edge of a dense region. Unlike a core point, which starts and expands dense regions, a border point can be attached to a dense region but does not expand the cluster. This limitation exists because direct density-reachability requires the starting point to be a core point; consequently, a core point can directly reach a border point, but a border point cannot directly reach back as a core-expanding point. A border point can fall within the neighborhoods of several core points, which can create ambiguity in cluster assignment if those core points belong to different clusters. In such cases, a border tie occurs, and the standard algorithm requires a convention to resolve it, such as assigning the border point to the first cluster that reaches it or using a nearest-core rule as a deterministic tie-breaker. In the informal description of the clustering algorithm, any border point that is close enough to a core point is put in the same cluster as that core point. Border points are distinct from noise points, which are neither core nor border points and are discarded or ignored by the cluster structure.

contextual_kc_draft.text:
In the context of density-based clustering, specifically DBSCAN, a noise point is defined as any data point that is neither a core point nor a border point. This classification arises from a center-based approach to density, which categorizes points into three distinct types: those in the interior of a dense region (core points), those on the edge of a dense region (border points), and those in sparsely occupied regions (noise or background points). A noise point is characterized by its location in a low-density region, meaning it does not have enough neighbors within the specified radius to be considered a core point, nor is it within the radius of any core point to be considered a border point.

In the DBSCAN algorithm, noise points are treated distinctly from clustered points. While core points are used to form and expand clusters, and border points are attached to existing clusters, noise points are discarded or ignored by the cluster structure. This mechanism allows DBSCAN to automatically classify low-density points as noise and remove them from the clustering process, thereby mitigating the negative effects that outliers or random measurement errors can have on clustering performance. The identification of noise points is sensitive to the algorithm's parameters; for instance, if the neighborhood radius (epsilon) is set too small, many points may be classified as noise, whereas if the minimum points threshold (minPts) is set too large, real small clusters may disappear as noise.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Noise and Outliers An atypical point (outlier) can often severely degrade the performance of clustering algorithms, especially algorithms such as K-means that are prototype-based. On the other hand, noise can cause techniques, such as single link, to join clusters that should not be joined. In some cases, algorithms for removing noise and outliers are applied before a clustering algorithm is used. Alternatively, some algorithms can detect points that represent noise and outliers during the clustering process and then delete them or otherwise eliminate their negative effects. In the previous chapter, for instance, we saw that DBSCAN automatically classifies low-density points as noise and removes them from the clustering process. Chameleon ( Section 8.4.4 ), SNN density-based clustering ( Section 8.4.9 ), and CURE ( Section 8.5.3 ) are three of the algorithms in this chapter that explicitly deal with noise and outliers during the clustering process.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: Given the previous definitions of core points, border points, and noise points, the DBSCAN algorithm can be informally described as follows. Any two core points that are close enough—within a distance Eps of one another—are put in the same cluster. Likewise, any border point that is close enough to a core point is put in the same cluster as the core point. (Ties need to be resolved if a border point is close to core points from different clusters.) Noise points are discarded. This algorithm uses the same concepts and finds the same clusters as the original DBSCAN, but is optimized for simplicity, not efficiency.

contextual_kc_draft.text: DBSCAN requires two user-specified parameters, Eps and MinPts, to define its density-based clustering behavior. Unlike K-means, which requires the number of clusters to be specified, DBSCAN automatically determines the number of clusters but relies on these two parameters to establish density connectivity. Eps defines the radius of the neighborhood around a point, while MinPts specifies the minimum number of points required within that neighborhood for a point to be classified as a core point. The point itself is included in the count of points within the Eps radius. A point is considered a core point if there are at least MinPts points within a distance of Eps. The selection of these parameters is critical because DBSCAN uses one global Eps and one global MinPts for the entire dataset. A common method for determining these values involves computing the k-dist (the distance from a point to its k-th nearest neighbor) for all data points, sorting them in increasing order, and plotting the sorted values. A sharp increase in this plot indicates a suitable value for Eps, while the value of k used in the calculation serves as the MinPts parameter. This approach helps distinguish between points belonging to clusters, which have small k-dist values, and noise points, which have relatively large k-dist values. However, DBSCAN can struggle when cluster densities vary widely, as a single global Eps threshold may fail to correctly identify all clusters or may merge distinct clusters into one. For example, if Eps is chosen to separate two dense clusters, it might cause two less dense clusters to be labeled as noise, or vice versa. The original DBSCAN algorithm often used a value of k=4, which appears reasonable for most two-dimensional data sets, though the optimal Eps value depends on the specific data and the chosen k.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: There is, of course, the issue of how to determine the parameters Eps and MinPts . The basic approach is to look at the behavior of the distance from a point to its nearest neighbor, which we will call the k -dist. For points that belong to some cluster, the value of k -dist will be small if k is not larger than the cluster size. Note that there will be some variation, depending on the density of the cluster and the random distribution of points, but on average, the range of variation will not be huge if the cluster densities are not radically different. However, for points that are not in a cluster, such as noise points, the k -dist will be relatively large. Therefore, if we compute the k -dist for all the data points for some k , sort them in increasing order, and then plot the sorted values, we expect to see a sharp change at the value of k -dist that corresponds to a suitable value of Eps . If we select this distance as the Eps parameter and take the value of k as the MinPts parameter, then points for which k -dist is less than Eps will be labeled as core points, while other points will be labeled as noise or border points.

evidence_for_synthesis.source_block_text: DBSCAN can have trouble with density if the density of clusters varies widely. Consider Figure 7.24 , which shows four clusters embedded in noise. The density of the clusters and noise regions is indicated by their darkness. The noise around the pair of denser clusters, A and B , has the same density as clusters C and D . For a fixed MinPts , if the Eps threshold is chosen so that DBSCAN finds C and D as distinct clusters, with the points surrounding them as noise, then A and B and the points surrounding them will become a single cluster. If the Eps threshold is set so that DBSCAN finds A and B as separate clusters, and the points surrounding them are marked as noise, then C , D , and the points surrounding them will also be marked as noise.
